query: Why does God allow suffering? What is the Christian answer to evil and pain?
rationale: broad; every collection has material

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Nearly every chunk engages the problem of evil/suffering directly: CCC 309-314 (providence and the scandal of evil, twice), Spe Salvi 36-37 (suffering as part of human existence), Deus Caritas Est 38 (Job), Summa I.2.3 ad 1 (Augustine's 'good out of evil'), Summa I.48.2 (whether evil is found in things), Lactantius Chap. XXIX (why does God permit these things), Lumen Fidei 57 (faith and the suffering), and Pauline passages on suffering producing endurance/consolation. The two Cyprian treatise chunks and the pseudo-Cyprian Treatise II shift toward persecution/martyrdom — suffering endured for the faith and its testing purpose — which is an adjacent but narrower topic than the general theodicy question; the pseudo-Cyprian rack/red-hot-plates passage is the weakest, being about martyrdom's purpose rather than the origin or meaning of evil generally. Still, these remain within the 'why does God permit affliction' theme rather than a different doctrine, so no true vocabulary collision (no chunk is about, say, mortification of the flesh or penance as a distinct doctrine). Relevance is high with a few peripheral drifts.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Collection by collection: Catechism — CCC §309–314 is precisely the canonical 'Providence and the scandal of evil' treatment, and a second part of the same section is retrieved; excellent, though CCC §385 (Where does evil come from?) and §§1500ff on illness were not found. Summa — I.2.3 ad 1 (Augustine's dictum) and I.48.2 (whether evil is found in things) are genuinely core theodicy passages; I.19.9 (whether God wills evils) and I.48.1 (evil as privation) would be even more canonical, but these are strong. Papal encyclicals — Spe Salvi §§36–37 is the canonical modern treatment of suffering and hope; Deus Caritas Est §38 on Job is apt; Lumen Fidei §57 is solid though more peripheral. Scripture — Romans 5:1–5, Romans 8:28–34, 2 Cor 1:3–11, 1 Pet 4:12–19 are all central suffering texts, though Romans 8:18–27 (the groaning of creation, arguably the single most canonical passage) and Job itself are absent. Patristics — Lactantius Chap. XXIX is a direct 'why does God permit' passage; the Cyprian chunks are mid-tier persecution-focused. Overall strong canonical hits in most collections with a few notable misses (Salvifici Doloris entirely absent, no Job).

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation, systematic/philosophical (theodicy), magisterial/catechetical definition, pastoral application, historical/patristic precedent. All five are represented: Scripture (Romans 5, Romans 8, 2 Cor 1, 1 Peter 4), systematic (two Summa articles on God permitting evil and evil in things), magisterial/catechetical (CCC §309–314 twice), pastoral (Spe Salvi 36–37, Lumen Fidei 57 on Mother Teresa and the leper, Deus Caritas Est 38), and historical/patristic (Lactantius, Cyprian). This clearly exceeds three distinct angles.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The doctrine has real tension: evil as privation with no positive cause and God not willing evil, versus God permitting evil to draw greater good; and the tension between reducing/resisting suffering versus redemptive acceptance of it. Both poles appear: Augustine's 'bring good even out of evil' and Summa I.48.2 on the perfection of the whole handle the permissive side; CCC 309-314 affirms the mystery and rejects quick answers; Spe Salvi explicitly says 'we must do whatever we can to reduce suffering' while also warning against fleeing it, capturing the resist/embrace tension; Romans 8:28 supplies the providential good. What is thin is the account of evil's origin — human freedom and the Fall (CCC §385 or §410–412) is absent, so the moral-evil-from-free-will pole and the Christological answer (Christ's Passion as the definitive answer, Salvifici Doloris) are underrepresented, with the Cyprian/pseudo-Cyprian chunks tilting the set toward 'suffering as testing,' one particular pole. Solid but not fully balanced.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source repeats: two chunks of CCC §309–314 — the second ('the ways of his providence are often unknown to us... only at the end') adds the eschatological resolution rather than merely restating the first, so partially additive but overlapping in argument. Two Spe Salvi chunks (§36 and §37) are contiguous and both argue that suffering cannot be eliminated and must be embraced — significant overlap. Two Summa chunks are from different questions with distinct arguments. Two Cyprian Treatises chunks (Treatise VII and Chapter IX) both argue affliction serves to prove/strengthen us — the thorn-in-the-flesh passage and the 'afflictions arise for the sake of our being proved' passage make substantially the same point, plus pseudo-Cyprian Treatise II again says suffering is 'for the sake of trying us' (different work, but near-identical argument). Several overlapping pairs, though none are pure duplicates.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: Both poles are represented unusually well on the speculative side: Summa I.19.9 explicitly holds that God neither wills evil to be done nor wills it not to be — the precise nuance that God permits without willing evil — set beside Augustine's 'brings good even out of evil,' while CCC §385 raises the origin of evil in the context of the Fall and CCC §309–314 insists no quick answer suffices. scores.summary: Excellent doctrinal-core retrieval — CCC §309–314 plus §385, Summa I.19.9 on whether God wills evils, and Dilexit Nos add real depth and balance — but the scriptural angle misses Romans 8:18–27 and Job, and the tail is padded with three patristic passages all sounding the 'affliction as testing' note, including the lowest-scoring pseudo-Cyprian chunk.

judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines share a strong core (CCC §309–314, Summa I.2.3 ad 1, Spe Salvi §36, Deus Caritas Est §38 on Job, Lumen Fidei §57, Lactantius XXIX, Romans 5:1–5, Cyprian Ch. IX), so differences turn on what each adds in the unique slots.

hyde_haiku produces the most complete set: it uniquely adds CCC §410–412 (God's non-abandonment and promised victory over evil), Romans 8:18–27 — the single most canonical NT passage on present suffering versus future glory — 2 Cor 4:7–18, and a Job chapter, giving it the best scriptural foundation and the fullest doctrinal arc from Fall to eschatological hope. Its weaknesses are the contiguous Spe Salvi §36/§37 pair and two soft selections (Eliphaz's speech in Job 5, Augustine on the virtue of patience).

hyde_cohere_luna has the strongest speculative and catechetical core: CCC §385 ('Where does evil come from?') alongside §309–314, and Summa I.19.9 'Whether God wills evils,' which is the most precisely on-point Thomistic article for this query, plus Dilexit Nos §192 for a fresh magisterial angle. Its cost is the scriptural side — no Romans 8:18–27 and no Job text — and a tail of three patristic passages all making the 'affliction proves us' argument, ending with a 0.48-scoring pseudo-Cyprian martyrdom passage.

hyde_cohere_haiku is the weakest of the three. It duplicates CCC §309–314 across two slots, pairs Spe Salvi §36 with §37, and spends three slots on Cyprian/pseudo-Cyprian persecution-as-testing material, leaving it without any passage on the origin of evil (no CCC §385 or §410–412) and without the eschatological Romans 8:18–27. Its scriptural picks (Romans 8:28–34, 2 Cor 1, 1 Pet 4) are good but skew entirely toward consolation in trial rather than theodicy proper.

Notably, no pipeline retrieved Salvifici Doloris, the definitive magisterial document on the meaning of human suffering, nor any passage treating Christ's Passion as the definitive Christian answer to evil — a shared gap. Ranking: hyde_haiku strongest overall, hyde_cohere_luna a close second with better doctrinal depth but weaker scripture, hyde_cohere_haiku third due to redundancy and the missing origin-of-evil pole.

rationale: moral reasoning; should favour Summa + Catechism

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The core of the set is squarely on the query: CCC §2475–2487 (lying condemned by nature), CCC §2488–2492 (right to truth is not unconditional — directly relevant to 'is deception always wrong'), Summa II-II Q110 A1 and A3 (whether lying is always opposed to truth; whether every lie is a sin), Augustine's De Mendacio/Contra Mendacium material (Chs. 18, 22, Sections 5 and 38) which is precisely the classic treatise on whether lying is ever permissible, and Veritatis Splendor §§77 and 82 plus Evangelium Vitae §75 on intention vs. intrinsically evil object — exactly the 'does intention matter' half of the query. Joshua 2 (Rahab) and Joshua 9 (Gibeonite deception) are the standard scriptural test cases actually debated by Augustine and Aquinas on this very question, so they are on-topic rather than collisions, though thinner. Ephesians 4:17–32 ('putting away falsehood, speak truth with his neighbor') and Proverbs 12 (many verses on lying lips vs. truthful witness) are lexically and topically about truthfulness, so relevant if generic. Evangelium Vitae §75 is about absolute negative precepts generally rather than lying specifically — adjacent, but it is the exact principle governing the answer, and Veritatis Splendor supplies the same frame more directly. No chunk is about a different doctrine masquerading via shared vocabulary; the weakest items (Proverbs 12) are diffuse wisdom material rather than a wrong doctrine. So: mostly tightly on-concept with two or three generic-but-related scriptural fillers.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection: Catechism — found both §2475–2487 (the direct 'lying is to be condemned' treatment) and §2488–2492 ('the right to the communication of the truth is not unconditional'), which together are the canonical CCC treatment including the nuance; excellent. Summa — Q110 is exactly the question on lying; A1 (whether lying is always opposed to truth, with the object/end analysis) and A3 (whether every lie is a sin) are the two canonical articles; A2 on species of lies and A4 on mortal sin are missing but the core is captured. Augustine — Chapters 18 and 22 of Enchiridion plus Sections 5 and 38 of De Mendacio: these are the headline passages ('It is Never Allowable to Tell a Lie'; 'A Lie is Not Allowable, Even to Save Another from Injury'; 'whether a lie be at some times useful'); this is canonical. Veritatis Splendor — §77 (intention and consequences) and §82 (intention good only when object orderable to God) are the precise sections for the intention question; §79–80 on intrinsically evil acts would be equally canonical but §82 substantially covers it. Scripture — Joshua 2 Rahab is the canonical hard case; Ephesians 4 and Proverbs 12 are mid-tier; the more canonical texts (Exodus 20 false witness, Ex 23:1, Rev 21:8, John 8:44) are not present. Averaging: strong canonical hits in every doctrinal collection, mid-tier in scripture.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles for a moral-theology question like this: scriptural foundation, systematic/philosophical reasoning, magisterial definition, historical/patristic precedent, and pastoral application. Scriptural: Joshua 2, Joshua 9, Ephesians 4, Proverbs 12. Systematic: Summa Q110 A1 and A3 (object/end analysis). Magisterial: CCC §§2475–2492, Veritatis Splendor §§77, 82, Evangelium Vitae §75. Patristic/historical: four Augustine passages including the record of the dispute ('some asserting that it is never right to lie... others gainsaying'). Pastoral: CCC §2488–2492 on discretion, professional secrets, and when it is appropriate to reveal truth supplies genuine pastoral application. That is four to five distinct angles, well beyond the three-angle threshold.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The real tension here is (a) lying is intrinsically evil and never permitted, versus (b) one is not always obliged to disclose the truth — mental reservation, professional secrecy, the right to privacy, and the classic hard cases. Pole one is amply present (CCC §2475ff, Summa A3, Augustine Chs. 18 and 22, Section 38, Veritatis Splendor §82, Evangelium Vitae §75 on exceptionless negative precepts). Pole two is genuinely present: CCC §2488–2492 explicitly states the right to communication of truth is not unconditional and grounds discretion and secrecy; Summa A1's object/end distinction and Veritatis Splendor §77's acknowledgment that intention must be taken into account supply the nuance on intention; Augustine Section 5 raises whether a lie can be useful and whether it is a lie absent will to deceive; Joshua 2 and 9 present the scriptural counter-examples. The gradation of culpability (jocose/officious lies, gravity by circumstance) is only partly present — Augustine Ch. 18's heading flags it and CCC mentions culpability, but the Summa's A2/A4 treatment of species and mortal-vs-venial is absent. Nearly both poles, with a small gap on gradation of gravity.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs to check. Augustine appears four times but from distinct works and with distinct arguments: Ch. 18 (never allowable but guilt differs by intention/subject), Ch. 22 (not even to save another from injury), Section 5 (whether a lie may be useful; definition without will to deceive), Section 38 (surveying the dispute). Chapter 22 and Section 38 both land on 'never lie,' which is mild overlap, but each adds distinct reasoning and material. Summa A1 and A3 are different articles making different arguments (species of the act from object and end; versus lying as inordinate and impermissible even to avert harm). CCC §2475–2487 and §2488–2492 are complementary, not repetitive — one prohibits, the other qualifies. Veritatis Splendor §77 and §82 both address intention, with §82 restating the primacy of object over intention that §77 sets up — modest overlap. Evangelium Vitae §75 converges with Veritatis Splendor §82 but is a different source, which is not penalized. Overall only slight same-source overlap.

Both poles of the doctrine are represented and multiple angles are covered; only mild same-source overlap and a few generic wisdom-literature fillers at the tail.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The top half is excellent and directly on-concept: Augustine Chs. 18 and 22, Summa Q110 A1 and A3, two CCC chunks from §2475–2487, Augustine Sections 25 and 42 (the taxonomy of eight kinds of lies and the conclusion that Scripture never sanctions lying), and Joshua 2 (Rahab). Exodus 23:1–9 ('You shall not spread a false report... shall not testify to pervert justice') is genuinely on the ethics of false speech. But the tail drifts. Proverbs 6:1–19 is largely about surety, sloth, and the seven abominations — only a couple of clauses touch lying; it is a diffuse chapter retrieved on vocabulary. Sirach 5 is about presumption, delay in repentance, and self-confidence, with only glancing reference to speech — largely off-concept. Most seriously, Veritatis Splendor §62 and §63 are about the erroneous conscience and invincible ignorance — a genuinely different moral-theological doctrine that shares the vocabulary of 'truth,' 'error,' and 'mistaken.' Neither section addresses lying, deception, or the object/intention structure of the act; they address the binding force and dignity of conscience. That is a vocabulary collision on 'truth/error,' and it displaces the sections (§§77–82) that actually answer the intention half of the query. Two collision chunks plus two diffuse wisdom chunks materially degrade the set.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Catechism: two chunks from the same §2475–2487 range — one the 'lying is to be condemned' passage, the other the 'Offenses Against Truth' opening on false witness and perjury; both are on-target, but §2488–2492 (respect for truth, the non-unconditional right to it, professional secrets) — the section that most directly answers 'is deception always wrong' — was not found, a real miss. Summa: Q110 A1 and A3 are canonical; well selected. Augustine: Chs. 18 and 22 plus Sections 25 and 42 — Section 25's ranking of the kinds of lies and Section 42's conclusion are canonical De Mendacio material; very good. Veritatis Splendor: §§62–63 on conscience are peripheral for this query while §§77–82 on intention and intrinsically evil acts — the encyclical's canonical treatment of exactly this issue, and demonstrably present in the corpus since sibling pipelines retrieved them — were missed. That is close to the 0.0 anchor for that collection. Scripture: Joshua 2 is the canonical hard case and Exodus 23 is a strong Decalogue-adjacent text, but Proverbs 6 and Sirach 5 are peripheral. Averaging strong Summa/Augustine, good-but-incomplete CCC, and a badly selected Veritatis Splendor.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural, systematic, magisterial, patristic/historical, pastoral. Scriptural: Joshua 2, Exodus 23, Proverbs 6, Sirach 5 — heavily represented. Systematic: Summa Q110 A1 and A3. Magisterial: CCC §2475–2487 (twice) and Veritatis Splendor §§62–63. Patristic: Augustine Chs. 18, 22 and Sections 25, 42. So four distinct angles are present, clearing the three-angle bar. Pastoral application is the thin spot: nothing here addresses the concrete practice of discretion, secrecy, or how to withhold truth charitably, since CCC §2488–2492 is absent; Veritatis Splendor §§62–63 on conscience formation offers a faint substitute. Coverage is broad but scripture-heavy and pastorally thin.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The absolutist pole is overwhelmingly represented: Augustine Ch. 18, Ch. 22, Section 42 ('we must never at all tell a lie'), Summa A3, CCC §2475ff twice, Exodus 23, Proverbs 6. The balancing pole is thin. There is genuine nuance in Augustine Section 25's ranking of lies by gravity and in Summa A3's reply about the jocose lie not intended to deceive, plus Summa A1's object/end distinction — so gradation of culpability is present. But the crucial qualification that the right to know the truth is not unconditional, and that discretion, mental reservation, and professional secrecy are legitimate — CCC §2488–2492 — is entirely missing, and Veritatis Splendor's treatment of the role of intention (§77) is likewise missing, replaced by conscience passages. Joshua 2 stands alone as the counter-case with no source that adjudicates it favorably. A user reading only this set would conclude that deception is always wrong with no sense of the licit ways of withholding truth. Dominant side well covered; balancing pole present only faintly via gradation-of-gravity material.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Two chunks come from the same CCC range §2475–2487; they are adjacent sections making related but not identical points (the general condemnation of lying and the profanation of speech; versus false witness and perjury as specific offenses) — modest but real overlap of substance. Augustine's four chunks are largely distinct: Ch. 18 (never allowable, guilt varies), Ch. 25 (hierarchy of eight lies), Ch. 22 and Section 42 both concluding that lying is never permissible even to help another — that pair is a fairly close restatement of the same absolutist thesis from the same author. Summa A1 and A3 are distinct articles. Veritatis Splendor §62 and §63 are consecutive sections both about the erroneous conscience and the dignity of conscience deriving from truth — substantially the same argument, effectively a wasted slot. So there are two or three same-source pairs with meaningful overlap.

scores.summary: Strong on Augustine and the Summa, with four distinct patristic passages and both canonical Q110 articles, but the set drifts badly at the tail: Veritatis Splendor §§62–63 on the erroneous conscience is a different doctrine retrieved on shared 'truth/error' vocabulary, and Proverbs 6 and Sirach 5 are diffuse. Missing CCC §2488–2492 and Veritatis Splendor §§77/82 leaves the qualifying pole — the licit withholding of truth and the role of intention — largely unrepresented, and there is same-source repetition in the CCC and Veritatis Splendor pairs.

judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines share a strong doctrinal core — CCC §2475–2487, Augustine's Enchiridion Chs. 18 and 22, and Joshua 2 (Rahab) — and all correctly identify that this query requires both the Summa's Q110 on lying and Augustine's dedicated treatises. They diverge sharply on how well they handle the second half of the question ('does intention matter?') and the qualifying pole of the doctrine.

hyde_cohere_haiku and hyde_cohere_luna both retrieve CCC §2488–2492 ('the right to the communication of the truth is not unconditional') and Veritatis Splendor §§77 and 82 (intention vs. the moral object), which are precisely the passages that answer whether intention can change the morality of deception and when truth may legitimately be withheld. Both therefore achieve near-complete doctrinal balance. hyde_cohere_haiku edges ahead on completeness by adding Summa Q110 A4 (whether every lie is a mortal sin — the gradation of gravity) and Augustine Section 33 (the Egyptian midwives and the women of Jericho, i.e., the biblical counter-cases adjudicated directly), giving the fullest affirmation-plus-nuance picture. hyde_cohere_luna compensates with Summa A1's object/end analysis, the strongest single systematic passage, and slightly better scriptural framing via Proverbs 12 over Proverbs 19.

hyde_haiku has the best patristic depth of the three — Augustine Sections 25 (hierarchy of kinds of lies) and 42 alongside the two Enchiridion chapters — and pairs both canonical Summa articles. But it substitutes Veritatis Splendor §§62–63 on the erroneous conscience for §§77/82 on intention. Those conscience sections are a different moral-theological doctrine retrieved on shared 'truth/error' vocabulary, a genuine collision that also wastes two slots on near-identical consecutive sections. Combined with the absence of CCC §2488–2492 and two diffuse wisdom chunks (Proverbs 6, Sirach 5), hyde_haiku presents a one-sidedly absolutist picture that omits the legitimate withholding of truth. It is the weakest on relevance, best-passage selection, completeness, and redundancy, despite its strong top half.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles for a doctrinal 'what does the Church teach' query: scriptural foundation, systematic/philosophical reasoning, magisterial/catechetical definition, historical/patristic precedent, and pastoral application (devotion to guardian angels, veneration). What is thinner is the pastoral/positive pole: guardian angels and the Church's veneration/invocation of angels in the liturgy is absent, and the metaphysical claim of pure spirituality is only implicit in CCC §328 rather than developed (no Summa Q50/51). Augustine XI.9 and XI.32 both concern the creation of the angels and XI.32 substantially reworks XI.9's exegesis of 'let there be light' — meaningful overlap in the same argument. 2 Peter 2:4–9 and 2:10–22 are adjacent chunks of the same passage both on the fallen/judged angels — a genuine redundant pair. scores.summary: Strong core angelology from Catechism, Augustine, Origen, Aquinas and Scripture with broad angle coverage, but the set is marred by three off-topic chunks — including a pure lexical collision on 'Angelic Doctor' in Humani Generis — and by adjacent-chunk redundancy in 2 Peter and City of God.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The top of the list is excellent and precisely on the concept: CCC §329–330 (Augustine's 'angel is the name of their office, not their nature'), CCC §328 (existence as truth of faith), Augustine XI.9 and XI.32 on the creation of angels, Summa Q51 a.1 (angels have no bodies) and Q54 a.5 (only intellectual knowledge in angels), Tobit 12 (Raphael reveals himself — the paradigmatic angelic-ministry narrative), Psalm 148 ('praise him, all his angels'), Origen Against Celsus V.4, Hebrews 1, 2 Peter 2:4 on fallen angels. Irenaeus Against Heresies I.10 is a rule-of-faith summary that does touch the invisible creation and the angels' subjection to Christ, so it is thematically defensible if broad. The two clear off-doctrine passages constitute vocabulary/theme collisions that pull the score down, though there is no jarring wrong-doctrine hit like 'Angelic Doctor'.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Catechism: it found both §328 and §329–330, i.e. the definitional heart of the CCC's treatise on angels (existence as a truth of faith, and their nature as spirits/office as messengers) — essentially the canonical answer. Summa: Q51 a.1 on whether angels have bodies naturally united to them is a core angelology article, and Q54 a.5 on purely intellectual knowledge is likewise central to the treatise on angels; only Q50 a.1 (altogether incorporeal) would be more canonical. Good vs. fallen angels: 2 Peter 2:4 supplies the fallen pole. Subordination to Christ and prohibition of worship: Hebrews 1 and Irenaeus' rule of faith give the guard against angel-veneration excess. Summa Q51 a.1 and Q54 a.5 address different questions (corporeality vs. mode of knowledge) — distinct. judge.comparative_analysis:

judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines converge on a strong shared spine — Augustine's Confessions XIII.13–14 ('O my God, Where art Thou?'), Lamentations 3, Lumen Fidei §56, Deus Caritas Est §38 on Job and divine silence — and all three achieve full multi-angle coverage across scripture, systematic theology, magisterial documents, pastoral guidance, and patristic precedent. hyde_haiku has the best doctrinal instincts: it ranks CCC §2729–2733, the Catechism's explicit treatment of dryness and its discernment between purificatory dryness and dryness from unconverted living, in first position, and pairs it with the sharpest lament psalms (77, 13) and complementary pastoral material (Lumen Fidei §57, Dilexit Nos §157, Sirach 2). But it misses CCC §2729–2733 entirely, substituting adjacent prayer sections, which costs it on best-passage selection and leaves the dryness-versus-tepidity discernment only implicit.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Nearly every chunk engages the specific question of when conscience/divine law overrides obedience to human authority: ST II-II q104 a5 (obedience limits), EV §74 (unjust laws and conscience/cooperation), Pacem in Terris §51 (unjust laws not binding), ST I-II q96 a4 (does human law bind conscience), EV §72 (conformity of civil law to moral law), Libertas §13 (obedience to just law — the balancing pole, still directly on topic), Origen V.37 (two laws, natural vs. written), Acts 5 and Daniel 3 (canonical scriptural refusals), Daniel 1 (Daniel's refusal to defile himself — slightly more devotional/dietary but still an act of principled non-compliance), CCC §1777–1782 and §1795–1802 (judgment of conscience — the conscience side, directly applicable), 1 Peter 2 (submission pole), Origen VIII.65 (refusing impiety to please kings), Augustine Section 23 (bishop refusing imperial command — historical precedent). The Cyprian Epistle XXV chunk is the weakest: it is an exhortation on martyrdom/confession under torture, addressing perseverance and heavenly reward rather than the moral logic of when conscience obligates disobedience; it is adjacent (martyrdom presupposes refusal to obey) rather than a different doctrine, so not a true vocabulary collision. CCC conscience chunks are about conscience formation generally rather than conscience vs. civil authority specifically, which is mildly adjacent. Overall on-topic with one or two adjacent passages.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection: Summa — found I-II q96 a4 (the canonical article on whether human law binds conscience) and II-II q104 a5 (canonical article on limits of obedience), though the q104 chunk is only the 'On the contrary' fragment rather than the fuller respondeo, which is a slight downgrade. Evangelium Vitae — §72 and §74 are core to the unjust-law/conscientious-cooperation treatment, but the single most canonical line ('no obligation in conscience to obey such laws... grave and clear obligation to oppose them by conscientious objection', §73) was missed. Pacem in Terris — §51 is exactly the canonical passage. CCC — §1777–1782 and §1795–1802 are the core conscience sections, but §2242 ('the citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow the directives of civil authorities when they are contrary to the moral order') is the single most canonical Catechism passage for this query and was not retrieved. Scripture — Acts 5:29 and Daniel 3 are the canonical loci. Patristics — Origen V.37 and Augustine's Firmus story are apt; Cyprian is peripheral. So most collections yield strong-to-canonical passages, with two notable near-misses (CCC 2242, EV 73) and one truncated Summa fragment.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation, systematic/philosophical reasoning, magisterial/papal teaching, pastoral application, historical precedent. Scriptural: Acts 5, Daniel 3, Daniel 1, 1 Peter 2. Systematic: Aquinas on human law binding conscience and limits of obedience. Magisterial: Pacem in Terris, Evangelium Vitae, Libertas, plus CCC. Pastoral application: EV §74's treatment of concrete cooperation problems and CCC conscience formation. Historical precedent: Origen contra Celsus, Augustine's Bishop Firmus, Cyprian on confessors under persecution. This spans five distinct angles substantively.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The doctrine has real tension: a presumptive duty of obedience to legitimate authority versus the duty to disobey unjust commands. Both poles appear strongly: the obedience pole via Libertas §13 ('highest duty is to respect authority... whosoever resisteth authority resisteth the ordinance of God'), 1 Peter 2:13–20, and Aquinas's affirmation that just laws bind in conscience; the disobedience pole via Acts 5:29, Pacem in Terris §51, EV §72/§74, Daniel. Missing nuance: nothing explicitly on the erroneous/ill-formed conscience needing formation in relation to law (CCC §1790–1794 or Veritatis Splendor), and Romans 13 — the strongest text for the obedience pole — is absent, though 1 Peter and Libertas substitute. Also the distinction that unjust law may still be obeyed to avoid scandal/greater disorder (Aquinas I-II q96 a4 does contain this, so partially present).

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: EV §72 and §74 — related but distinct (§72 establishes the conformity-of-civil-law principle citing John XXIII; §74 addresses cooperation and conscientious objection in practice), so limited overlap. CCC §1777–1782 and §1795–1802 overlap substantially — the 'IN BRIEF' section is essentially a summary restatement of the judgment-of-conscience material, a genuinely redundant pair. Origen appears twice (V.37 on two laws; VIII.65 on refusing impious flattery of kings) with distinct arguments. Daniel 1 and Daniel 3 are different episodes but make the same substantive point (refusing a royal decree that violates God's law), a mild same-source overlap. One clear redundant pair plus one mild one.

scores.summary: A well-balanced, multi-angle result set that captures both poles of the obedience/conscience tension across Aquinas, papal encyclicals, Scripture, and patristic precedent. Weaknesses: the ST q104 chunk is only the 'On the contrary' fragment, the two most canonical single passages (CCC §2242 and EV §73) are missed, the Cyprian martyrdom chunk is peripheral, and the paired CCC conscience chunks are largely redundant.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Strong direct engagement across the board: EV §73 is the single most on-point magisterial statement ('no obligation in conscience to obey such laws... grave and clear obligation to oppose them by conscientious objection'); ST I-II q96 a4 and II-II q104 a5 (the full respondeo, better than a fragment) are the core systematic treatments; CCC §2238–2243 is precisely the Catechism's section on duties of citizens including the limits of civil obedience; Pacem in Terris §51, Romans 13, 1 Peter 2, Daniel 3 (both halves), Quod Nunquam §10, Etsi Multa §16 (civil law is not the norm of conscience — directly on point), Clement of Rome ch. CCC §1795–1802 is general conscience material, mildly adjacent. best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection this is the strongest selection: Evangelium Vitae — §73, the canonical conscientious-objection passage. CCC — §2238–2243, which contains §2242, the Catechism's canonical statement that the citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow directives contrary to the moral order; this is the best possible CCC chunk. Summa — I-II q96 a4 respondeo and II-II q104 a5 respondeo, both canonical and substantive rather than fragmentary. Pacem in Terris §51 — canonical. Scripture — Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2 for the obedience pole, Daniel 3 for refusal; Acts 5:29 (the locus classicus) is absent in its scriptural form, though its substance is quoted inside Quod Nunquam. Patristics — Origen, Clement, Tertullian are reasonable historical witnesses, with Tertullian's De Fuga being a weaker choice than, say, Origen V.37 on the two laws. multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Scriptural: Romans 13, 1 Peter 2, Daniel 3 (two chunks). Systematic/philosophical: two Aquinas articles with full respondeo reasoning. doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: Both poles are represented with unusual balance: the obedience pole via Romans 13:1–7 (the strongest scriptural text for submission), 1 Peter 2:13–20, and CCC §2238–2243's affirmation that citizens should regard authority as representing God and pay taxes/exercise the vote; the disobedience pole via EV §73, Pacem in Terris §51, Etsi Multa §16, Aquinas's unjust-law analysis, Daniel, and the martyr witnesses. redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: Daniel 3:8–18 and 3:19–30 are consecutive halves of one narrative making the same substantive point about refusing an idolatrous decree — the second chunk adds mainly the deliverance outcome, so this is a genuine same-source redundancy occupying a slot. scores.summary: The strongest set overall: it lands the canonical passages in nearly every collection (EV §73, CCC §2242 section, both Aquinas respondeos, Pacem in Terris §51), balances Romans 13/1 Peter submission against the duty of conscientious objection, and spans all five applicable angles. Costs: the split Daniel narrative and two closely-related Origen chunks waste slots, and the Tertullian De Fuga chunk is only tangential.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Top of the list is highly targeted: Pacem in Terris §51, EV §73 (the canonical conscientious-objection statement), ST I-II q96 a4 respondeo plus its Reply to Objection 2 ('in such matters human law should not be obeyed'), Libertas §13 (obedience pole), Origen V.37 (two laws), Acts 5:24–32 (locus classicus 'we must obey God rather than men'), CCC §1786–1789 (choosing in accord with conscience — directly relevant to when conscience binds), Daniel 3 and Daniel 1, Origen VIII.56 (never consenting to obey the laws of sin), CCC §1777–1782, Pacem in Terris §49 (authority obliges in conscience only insofar as it shares God's authority — precise), Augustine's Bishop Firmus, 1 Peter 2 (submission pole). The Tertullian De Fuga chunk (scored 0.36) about bribing a soldier and the denarius owed to Caesar is off-point for the conscience-versus-law principle, and Daniel 1's dietary self-restraint is more devotional purity than legal disobedience. best_passage_selection.reasoning: Summa — q96 a4 is canonical and the pipeline found both the respondeo and the pointed Reply to Objection 2, which is the sharpest single line; however II-II q104 a5 on obedience to superiors, squarely responsive to the 'authority' half of the query, was missed. Evangelium Vitae — §73 is the canonical passage. Pacem in Terris — §51 (canonical) plus §49 (the supporting principle), an excellent pairing. multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Scriptural: Acts 5, Daniel 3, Daniel 1, 1 Peter 2. Systematic/philosophical: two Aquinas chunks from q96 a4. scores.summary: A tightly relevant set that pairs the canonical magisterial and Thomistic passages with Acts 5 and strong patristic precedent, and uniquely supplies the erroneous-conscience nuance from CCC §1786–1789, giving it the most complete doctrinal picture. judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines converge on a strong shared core — Pacem in Terris §51, ST I-II q96 a4, Daniel 3, and 1 Peter 2:13–20 — which means all three capture the essential shape of the doctrine: legitimate authority binds in conscience, but a command contrary to the moral order does not bind and may oblige refusal.

They differ chiefly in best-passage selection and in which nuance they surface. hyde_haiku is the strongest on canonical retrieval: it is the only pipeline to find CCC §2238–2243, the Catechism section containing §2242's explicit statement on refusing directives contrary to the moral order, and it pairs the full respondeo of both relevant Summa articles (I-II q96 a4 on law binding conscience and II-II q104 a5 on limits of obedience) with EV §73 and Romans 13. Its Romans 13 + 1 Peter 2 + CCC civic-duty combination also gives the obedience pole its firmest scriptural grounding. Its weaknesses are redundancy — the Daniel 3 narrative split across two slots and two closely-related Origen chunks — and a tangential Tertullian passage.

hyde_cohere_luna has the sharpest doctrinal nuance: it alone retrieves CCC §1786–1789 on the erroneous conscience, which is the critical guardrail against reading 'conscience overrides obedience' subjectively, and it adds Pacem in Terris §49 for the underlying principle. But it spends two slots on the same Summa article (respondeo plus Reply to Obj. 2), misses ST II-II q104 on obedience to superiors entirely, misses CCC §2242, and carries the weakest single chunk in any set (Tertullian at 0.36).

hyde_cohere_haiku is the broadest across sources and uniquely surfaces EV §74's treatment of cooperation in evil — a genuinely useful pastoral angle — but it retrieves only the 'On the contrary' fragment of ST II-II q104 a5 rather than the reasoning, misses both EV §73 and CCC §2242, pairs two overlapping CCC conscience sections, and includes a peripheral Cyprian martyrdom exhortation.

Net: hyde_haiku leads on best-passage selection and coverage; hyde_cohere_luna leads on doctrinal completeness; hyde_cohere_haiku is the weakest of the three, chiefly through fragmentary and near-miss passage selection. No pipeline committed a true vocabulary collision — the weak chunks are adjacent (martyrdom, persecution-flight, dietary purity) rather than a different doctrine — so all three retain relevance scores above the collision threshold, differentiated by how many adjacent chunks each carries.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query has two parts: purpose of confession, and the mechanism of absolution. Chunk [1] (ST III q.84 a.3 on the form 'I absolve thee' and how sacraments effect what they signify) is precisely on the mechanism. [2] CCC 1468–1470 on the effects of the sacrament is directly on purpose. [3] CCC 1485–1498 IN BRIEF summarizes the whole sacrament including Jn 20:22-23. [4] Supplement q.18 a.1 on whether the power of the keys extends to remission of guilt — directly on how absolution works. [6] Ecclesia de Eucharistia §37 on Penance/Eucharist connection is adjacent but genuinely about the need for sacramental confession before communion. [7] Dives in Misericordia §13 on Penance as encounter with mercy — on purpose. [8] Charitate Christi §4 on penance as sacrament — relevant. [9] Augustine ch. 65 on God pardoning sins on condition of penitence — relevant historically. [10]-[12] three healing-of-the-paralytic parallels (Lk 5, Mk 2, Mt 9) — these are the classic scriptural warrant for Christ's authority on earth to forgive sins, so on-topic though thin per-passage. [5] Redemptor Hominis §20 on priesthood and self-giving is looser — it does touch the priest's role but leans toward priestly identity rather than absolution; borderline adjacency rather than a different doctrine. [14]-[16] the three Cyprian passages concern the lapsed, penitential discipline, and almsgiving as satisfaction — historically related to penance but Treatise VIII (almsgiving purging sin) and Treatise I (on unity/schism, resisting the Church) drift toward different subjects (schism, works of mercy) and are weakly connected to absolution's operation. No outright wrong-doctrine collision (nothing about, e.g., Baptism as a distinct doctrine or indulgences confused with absolution), but several tail chunks are peripheral rather than engaging the specific concept.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Catechism: two strong hits — CCC 1468–1470 (Effects of This Sacrament) and CCC 1485–1498 (IN BRIEF, which includes the institution and the essential elements). These are close to canonical; arguably CCC 1441–1449 (Christ forgives sins / reconciliation with the Church) and 1461–1467 (minister, the priest's role) are the very core for 'how absolution works,' and CCC 1446–1449 was missed here. Still, Effects + In Brief are strong. Summa: excellent — ST III q.84 a.3 on the form 'I absolve thee' is the canonical passage on the mechanism of absolution, plus Supplement q.18 a.1 on the power of the keys extending to remission of guilt. That is precisely the canonical treatment. Magisterial encyclicals: Dives in Misericordia §13 is the right section on Penance; Ecclesia de Eucharistia §37 is the right Penance section; Redemptor Hominis §20 is mid-tier. Scripture: the paralytic pericopes are the right kind of warrant, but Jn 20:19-23 as a standalone passage is absent (only quoted inside the CCC In Brief), which is the single most canonical scriptural passage for absolution. retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query is pastoral: grief-induced inability to pray, and whether that is spiritually acceptable. The strongest hits directly engage the two components — CCC §2729–2733 (difficulties in prayer: distraction, dryness) and CCC §2734–2741 (filial trust tested, 'some even stop praying') are precisely on target. Augustine Confessions IV.V is grief over the death of a friend, exactly the situation. Lamentations 3, Psalm 6, Psalm 55 are lament prayers that model bringing grief to God — on-topic and not merely vocabulary-sharing. Deus Caritas Est §38 (Job's complaint before God) and Dilexit Nos §161 (grief giving way to consolation) fit. Summa I-II q.37 a.3 on whether sorrow weakens all activity is a genuinely apt systematic account of why grief incapacitates action including prayer. Romans 8:35–39 is consolation-adjacent but relevant. Weaker: Lumen Fidei §56–57 are about faith and suffering/witness, thematically adjacent but not about inability to pray. The clearest misfire is Summa Supplement Q4 a.2 'whether it is expedient to grieve for sin continually' — this is contrition/penance grief over sin, a doctrinally distinct matter from bereavement grief; it shares only the word 'grieve.' That is a vocabulary collision on the wrong sense of sorrow. Confessions IV.XII is a general exhortation on loving mutable things in God — loosely related to the grief context but not to prayer difficulty.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Catechism: found the canonical passages — the CCC's actual treatment of 'difficulties in prayer' and of trust tested in tribulation, including the explicit note that some stop praying. That is the ideal answer passage. Augustine: Book IV Chapter V is the canonical grief-over-death lament in the Confessions; Chapter XII is a lesser but related section. Scripture: Psalms 6 and 55 and Lamentations 3:19–36 are strong lament selections, though Psalm 88 / Psalm 42 (the classic 'my tears have been my food... where is your God') and Job are arguably even more canonical for this pastoral situation and were missed. Aquinas: q.37 a.3 on sorrow weakening activity is the right locus; the Supplement contrition passage is peripheral and from a different treatise. Papal documents: Deus Caritas Est §38 and Dilexit Nos §161 are apt, but Spe Salvi's treatment of prayer and hope in suffering — and its section on prayer for the dead, highly relevant given a bereavement — was not found. Overall the core collections are represented at or near their best passages with some mid-tier filler.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation (laments), systematic/philosophical (Aquinas on the effects of sorrow), magisterial/catechetical (CCC on difficulties in prayer), pastoral application (encyclicals, Augustine's witness), historical/patristic precedent. This set covers scriptural (Psalms 6, 55, Lamentations 3, Romans 8), systematic (Summa q.37, Supplement q.4), catechetical/magisterial (CCC ×2), pastoral (Deus Caritas Est, Dilexit Nos, Lumen Fidei), and patristic/historical witness (Augustine ×2). doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The tension here is between permission/consolation (lament is legitimate prayer; dryness and inability are not sin; God receives the wordless cry) and the balancing pole (prayer remains a duty; perseverance in prayer matters; grief should not become despair or abandonment of God). The permissive/consoling pole is very strong: laments, Augustine's tears, Job's complaint, Dilexit Nos. The balancing pole is partially present: CCC §2734–2741 explicitly addresses those who stop praying and calls for filial trust and perseverance, and CCC §2729–2733 names dryness and the need for vigilance — this is the corrective pole. Also Aquinas provides the moderating note that sorrow does not necessarily shut out all movement. What is thinner is the eschatological/hope pole specific to bereavement — the Christian hope in resurrection and the practice of praying for the dead, which would reframe the mourner's relationship to prayer; that is absent. Still, both main poles are represented.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: CCC §2729–2733 and §2734–2741 are adjacent but make distinct arguments (distraction/dryness vs. filial trust tested and petition unheard) — complementary, not redundant. Psalms 6 and 55 are both individual laments crying out to God in distress; from the same collection with substantially overlapping substance, this is a mild redundancy. Confessions IV.V and IV.XII are different arguments (grief for the dead friend vs. loving creatures in God). Lumen Fidei §56 and §57 both argue that faith illuminates and speaks from within suffering — that pair overlaps significantly in substance. So roughly two same-source pairs with meaningful overlap out of fourteen slots.

scores.summary: Strong, wide-angled set that nails the Catechism's canonical treatment of difficulties in prayer and pairs it with laments, Aquinas on sorrow, and pastoral encyclicals; undercut by a vocabulary collision (Aquinas on continual grief for sin, a penitential rather than bereavement sorrow) and by two mildly redundant same-source pairs (Psalms 6/55, Lumen Fidei 56/57).

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Top result Spe Salvi §34 is directly about prayer as personal encounter sustained by the Church's prayers when one's own words fail — an excellent direct hit on 'I can't bring myself to pray.' Psalm 88 (the darkest lament, ending in darkness) and Psalm 42 ('my tears have been my food... where is your God') and Lamentations 3:1–18 and 3:19–36 are precisely the scriptural voice of a person who cannot pray in the ordinary way. multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural lament, systematic (Aquinas on the psychology of sorrow), magisterial/catechetical (CCC, Spe Salvi), pastoral (Spe Salvi, Dilexit Nos), patristic/historical (Augustine, Cyprian). All three pipelines share a solid core: the two CCC sections that are the corpus's canonical treatment of difficulties in prayer and of faltering trust in tribulation, Augustine's grief chapter, Lamentations 3:19–36, Deus Caritas Est §38 on Job's complaint, Dilexit Nos §161, and Summa I-II q.37 a.3 on sorrow weakening activity. rationale: inverts the suite's Summa gravity: encyclicals + Bible dominant

top.reference: Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part (Second Part of the Second Part) (Qq. 1–189), Question 118 - Of the Vices Opposed to Liberality, And in the First Place, OF COVETOUSNESS (EIGHT ARTICLES), Article 1 - Whether covetousness is a sin?

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query has two parts: the moral status of desiring wealth, and the concrete obligations of justice/charity toward the poor. Chunks [1] Populorum Progressio §23 (duty of rich toward poor, Ambrose on giving from what is the poor's own), [2] Fratelli Tutti §119 (universal destination of goods, Chrysostom), [3] Quadragesimo Anno §50 (superfluous income and the duty of almsgiving), [8] CCC §2443–2449 (Love for the Poor) are all bullseye on the second half. [4] Matthew 25:31–46 (sheep/goats, judgment on care for the least) directly grounds obligation. [5] Luke 18, [6] Mark 10, [7] Matthew 19 are the rich young ruler pericopes — directly on the danger of riches and the counsel to give to the poor, so on-topic, though three parallel synoptic accounts of the same episode. [9] Casti Connubii §119 is from an encyclical on marriage but the quoted passage is precisely about the rich's obligation to help needy families — relevant content though an odd source, not a doctrinal collision. [10] CCC §2551–2557 (tenth commandment in brief: avarice, envy, poverty of heart) speaks to disordered desire for riches — squarely on the first half. [11]/[14] Summa on covetousness as sin addresses whether wanting wealth is wrong. [12] Cyprian on lust of possessing, [13] Cyprian Testimony I (works of mercy), [15] Clement on rational use of riches all engage. [16] Augustine City of God I.10 on treasure in heaven/loss of possessions is the weakest — it is about the sack of Rome and the consolation of the faithful who lost goods, adjacent rather than about the morality of wealth-seeking or duties to the poor. That is one peripheral/tangential chunk, but not a different-doctrine vocabulary collision. Overall highly on-topic with one drift.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection: Catechism — CCC §2443–2449 'Love for the Poor' is the canonical passage for what one owes the poor, and §2551–2557 covers avarice/poverty of heart; however the canonical CCC treatment of the universal destination of goods (§2402–2406) and §2407 on temperance/justice in economic matters were not retrieved, which are core to 'what do I owe.' Social encyclicals — Populorum Progressio §23 and Quadragesimo Anno §50 are exactly the canonical loci; Fratelli Tutti §119 likewise. Scripture — Matthew 25 and the rich young man in all three synoptics are canonical texts; but 1 Timothy 6 ('those determined to be rich fall into a snare'; 'charge the rich...'), the single most directly responsive scriptural passage to 'is it wrong to want to be wealthy,' is missing. Summa — Q118 A1 on covetousness as sin is the right article, though the pipeline used two chunks of the same article rather than reaching A4 (mortal/venial) or the liberality question. Casti Connubii §119 is a peripheral locus for this topic when better encyclical passages exist. Strong but with notable canonical gaps.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation, systematic/philosophical reasoning, magisterial teaching, patristic/historical precedent, and pastoral application. Scriptural: Matthew 25, Luke 18, Mark 10, Matthew 19 — well covered. Magisterial/social teaching: Populorum Progressio, Fratelli Tutti, Quadragesimo Anno, Casti Connubii, CCC. Systematic: Summa Q118 on covetousness (two chunks). Patristic/historical: Cyprian (two), Clement, Augustine. Pastoral application: the CCC 'Love for the Poor' section and the encyclicals carry practical direction on almsgiving and superfluous income. Four to five distinct angles clearly present.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The doctrine has real tension: wealth is not evil in itself and private property is legitimate (goods rightly owned, stewardship, generosity as virtue), versus the universal destination of goods, the grave danger of riches, and the strict duty in justice — not merely charity — toward the poor. This set is heavily weighted to the demanding pole: duty of the rich, superfluous income belongs to the poor, judgment on the goats, sell what you have, covetousness is sin, lust of possessing not to be sought. The balancing pole is thin: Clement's 'riches are to be partaken of rationally' gestures at the legitimate use of wealth, and Summa Q118 A1 implies wealth is good in due measure, but there is no CCC §2402–2406 on the right to private property, no passage distinguishing the counsel of poverty from the precept binding all, and nothing affirming that seeking sufficiency and prosperity through honest labor is licit. A user could come away thinking desiring wealth is simply sinful.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Three synoptic parallels of the rich young ruler ([5] Luke 18, [6] Mark 10, [7] Matthew 19) are effectively the same pericope making the same point — these are distinct books but functionally the same source-text restated, consuming three of sixteen slots with near-identical content. Two chunks from the same Summa article Q118 A1 ([11] and [14]) both argue covetousness is a sin from due measure/regulation by reason — a same-source overlapping pair. Two Cyprian chunks are distinct in argument (Testimony LXI on lust of possessing vs. Testimony I on works of mercy). Two CCC chunks are distinct sections. So there is one clear same-source redundant pair plus a triple of near-duplicate gospel parallels.

scores.summary: Strong magisterial and patristic retrieval with excellent multi-angle spread, but wastes slots on three parallel synoptic accounts and a duplicated Summa article, misses 1 Timothy 6 and CCC §2402–2407, and leans one-sidedly toward condemnation of wealth without the legitimate-property/right-use pole.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Both halves of the question are directly served. [1] Rerum Novarum §22 addresses precisely the rich, the danger of riches, and the duty of almsgiving — a near-ideal answer to both halves. [2] Summa Q118 A1 on covetousness engages whether desiring wealth is sinful. [3] CCC §2443–2449 on love for the poor. [4] Matthew 19 rich young man. [5] Sirach 4 on not depriving the poor. [6] Cyprian on works of mercy. [7] CCC §2402–2406 universal destination and private ownership — exactly the doctrinal frame for what is owed. [8] Luke 12:13–21 the rich fool and 'beware covetousness' — directly on wanting wealth. [9] Quadragesimo Anno §50 superfluous income. [10] James 5:1–6 woe to the rich. [11] Cyprian Treatise VIII (On Works and Alms) on providence and almsgiving. [12] Lactantius answering the objection 'if I give all this away I'll have nothing' — remarkably responsive to the practical 'what do I actually owe' question. [13] Divini Redemptoris §44 detachment from earthly goods and charity. [14] Clement on rational use of riches. [15] Summa Q186 A3 on whether poverty is required for religious perfection — this is about the religious state and evangelical counsels, a distinct question from the layperson's morality of wealth; it does share vocabulary ('poverty', 'happiness') and is adjacent rather than a wrong-doctrine collision, but it is the weakest fit. [16] Divini Redemptoris §47 on the needy versus frivolous spending. Essentially all on-topic, one adjacent chunk on the counsel of poverty.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Catechism: both canonical loci appear — §2443–2449 (Love for the Poor) and §2402–2406 (universal destination and private ownership), which together are the core answer; only §2407 and the tenth-commandment avarice section are absent. Social encyclicals: Rerum Novarum §22 is the classic locus on the right use of riches and duty of almsgiving; Quadragesimo Anno §50 on superfluous income; Divini Redemptoris §§44 and 47 on detachment and charity. These are strong, central passages. Scripture: Matthew 19, Luke 12 (rich fool), James 5, Sirach 4 — good canonical wealth texts, though 1 Timothy 6:6–10/17–19, arguably the most on-point apostolic teaching for 'is it wrong to want to be wealthy,' is missing. Summa: Q118 A1 is the right article on covetousness; Q186 A3 on religious poverty is a lesser fit but does add the counsel/precept distinction. Patristics: Cyprian's De Opere et Eleemosynis (Treatise VIII) is the canonical patristic treatise on almsgiving — an excellent find; Lactantius VI.12 is the canonical classical treatment of mercy and its objections. Very good canonical hit rate across collections.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Scriptural: Matthew 19, Sirach 4, Luke 12, James 5. Magisterial: Rerum Novarum, Quadragesimo Anno, Divini Redemptoris (×2), CCC (×2). Systematic/philosophical: Summa Q118 on covetousness and Q186 on poverty and the twofold happiness. Patristic/historical: Cyprian (×2), Lactantius, Clement. Pastoral application: Lactantius's practical objection-and-answer about how much one can give away, Divini Redemptoris §47 on frivolous spending, CCC love for the poor. Five distinct angles are represented substantively.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: This set comes closest to holding both poles. The demanding pole is amply present (James 5, Quadragesimo Anno on superfluous income, Cyprian, Divini Redemptoris on detachment). Crucially the balancing pole also appears: CCC §2402–2406 affirms the legitimacy of private ownership alongside the universal destination of goods; Summa Q186 A3 distinguishes the perfection of poverty as a counsel of the religious state rather than a universal precept, which directly answers 'is it wrong to want to be wealthy' with nuance; Lactantius explicitly entertains the objection that total divestment is impossible and moderates it; Clement affirms riches rightly partaken of. Rerum Novarum §22 itself is the classic both-poles text (property is licit; use of it is a duty), though the retrieved excerpt emphasizes the warning to the rich. Still somewhat weighted toward warning, and nothing explicitly affirms the goodness of prosperity or a just wage/legitimate ambition, but the nuance is genuinely represented.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: two Divini Redemptoris chunks (§44 detachment/charity precept, §47 the needy versus frivolous spending) — related but making distinguishable points, mild overlap. Two Cyprian chunks are clearly distinct (Testimony I on the sheep-and-goats works of mercy vs. Treatise VIII on providence and almsgiving). Two CCC chunks are distinct sections (love for the poor vs. destination of goods/ownership). Two Summa chunks are different questions entirely (covetousness vs. religious poverty). No duplicated gospel parallels. Only one soft same-source overlap in sixteen results.

scores.summary: The most doctrinally balanced and least redundant set: it pairs the demanding social-justice pole with CCC §2402–2406 on private property, the Summa on poverty as counsel, and Lactantius answering the practical objection, while spanning all five applicable angles with canonical passages.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: [1] 1 Timothy 6:17–19 (charge the rich not to hope in riches but be rich in good works) and [7] 1 Timothy 6:6–10 ('those determined to be rich fall into a snare'; love of money the root of evils) are the single most precisely responsive scriptural texts to 'is it wrong to want to be wealthy' — a direct hit on the exact framing of the question. [2] CCC §2407 on temperance, justice, and solidarity in economic matters directly answers what is owed. [3] Summa Q118 A1 and [14] Q118 A4 (is covetousness always mortal?) address the culpability of desiring wealth with real precision. [4] CCC §2443–2449, [5] Quadragesimo Anno §50, [6] Populorum Progressio §23, [9] Fratelli Tutti §119, [10] A Quo Die §9 on mercy to the poor as the chief fruit of justice — all squarely on obligation. [8] Matthew 25 and [11] Mark 10 are canonical gospel texts. [12] Cyprian on lust of possessing, [13] Clement on rational use of riches, [15] Cyprian Testimony I on works of mercy all engage. [16] Augustine City of God I.10 (scored 0.38) is the outlier — about the faithful who lost property in Rome's sack and heavenly treasure, tangential to the moral question posed, and its very low score suggests weak match. No wrong-doctrine collision; one weak tail chunk.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Catechism: §2443–2449 (Love for the Poor) plus §2407 (temperance/justice/solidarity in economic matters) — both central, though §2402–2406 on the universal destination and private ownership, the doctrinal foundation for 'what I owe,' is missing. Scripture: 1 Timothy 6 in both halves is the canonical apostolic locus on desiring wealth, plus Matthew 25 and Mark 10 — an excellent, well-chosen scriptural core without wasteful parallels. Social encyclicals: Quadragesimo Anno §50, Populorum Progressio §23, Fratelli Tutti §119 — the canonical loci; A Quo Die §9 is a more obscure but genuinely on-point papal passage. Summa: two different articles of Q118 (A1 on covetousness as sin, A4 on mortal versus venial) — this is the collection's core treatment and the pipeline reached deeper into it than the others. Patristics: Cyprian Testimony LXI and Testimony I are apt florilegia entries, though Cyprian's dedicated treatise on almsgiving was not found; Augustine City of God I.10 is a peripheral pick for this topic. Overall the strongest passage selection on the scriptural and Summa side.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Scriptural: 1 Timothy 6 (×2), Matthew 25, Mark 10. Systematic/philosophical: Summa Q118 A1 and A4, with the mortal/venial distinction adding genuine moral-theological reasoning. Magisterial: Quadragesimo Anno, Populorum Progressio, Fratelli Tutti, A Quo Die, CCC (×2). Patristic/historical: Cyprian (×2), Clement, Augustine. Pastoral application: CCC §2407's practical virtue prescription and §2443–2449, plus 1 Timothy 6:17–19's direct pastoral charge to the rich. Four to five applicable angles substantively covered.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The nuanced pole is better served here than in hyde_cohere_haiku: 1 Timothy 6:17 explicitly says God 'richly provides us with everything to enjoy' and directs the rich to good works rather than condemning wealth as such; CCC §2407 frames the matter as temperance and justice in the use of goods rather than renunciation; Summa Q118 A4 makes the crucial distinction that covetousness is not always mortal sin, which directly moderates the answer to 'is it wrong to want to be wealthy'; Clement affirms riches rightly partaken of. Still, the affirmative doctrinal basis for private property and the universal destination of goods (CCC §2402–2406, or Rerum Novarum on the right to property) is absent, and the aggregate weight of Quadragesimo Anno, Populorum Progressio, Fratelli Tutti, Matthew 25 and Cyprian tilts strongly toward obligation and warning. Both poles are present but the balancing one is somewhat thin on the property-rights side.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: two 1 Timothy 6 chunks — but they make different arguments (6:6–10 warns against the determination to be rich; 6:17–19 instructs those already rich toward generosity and hope in God), so complementary rather than redundant. Two Summa Q118 chunks are different articles making different arguments (whether covetousness is a sin versus whether it is always mortal) — genuinely additive. Two CCC chunks are distinct sections. Two Cyprian chunks are distinct testimonies. Quadragesimo Anno, Populorum Progressio and Fratelli Tutti converge on the universal destination of goods, but these are three different sources, which counts as convergence across the tradition rather than redundancy. No wasteful same-source restatement, no duplicated gospel parallels.

scores.summary: The most precisely targeted set for this particular question, anchored by both halves of 1 Timothy 6, CCC §2407, and two distinct Summa articles including the mortal/venial nuance; efficient with almost no redundancy, weakened only by a stray Augustine chunk and the absence of CCC §2402–2406 on private property.

judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines share a solid core (Quadragesimo Anno §50, CCC §2443–2449, Summa Q118 A1, Cyprian Testimony I, Clement) and none commits an outright vocabulary collision — the retrieval space here is tight enough that the differences lie in efficiency and balance rather than in topical accuracy.

hyde_cohere_haiku is the weakest on efficiency and balance. It burns three of sixteen slots on the same rich-young-ruler pericope in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, and duplicates a single Summa article (Q118 A1) twice. Its encyclical picks are strong (Populorum Progressio, Fratelli Tutti), but it pulls an off-genre Casti Connubii passage and an Augustine chunk about the sack of Rome, and it entirely misses 1 Timothy 6 and CCC §2402–2407 — the two places the corpus most directly answers 'is it wrong to want to be wealthy' and 'what grounds my obligation.' The result reads as a one-sided warning against riches.

hyde_haiku is the most doctrinally complete. It uniquely retrieves CCC §2402–2406 (private ownership alongside the universal destination of goods), Summa Q186 A3 (poverty as a counsel of the religious state, not a universal precept), and Lactantius answering the practical objection that total divestment is impossible — three passages that together supply the nuance the other two lack. It also finds Cyprian's dedicated treatise on almsgiving and Rerum Novarum §22. Its only weaknesses are a mild Divini Redemptoris overlap and the absence of 1 Timothy 6.

hyde_cohere_luna is the most precisely targeted and least redundant. Both halves of 1 Timothy 6 map almost verbatim onto the user's two questions; CCC §2407 and two distinct Summa Q118 articles (including whether covetousness is always mortal) give it the sharpest moral-theological resolution. Every same-source pair is complementary rather than repetitive. It trails hyde_haiku only on doctrinal completeness, lacking the affirmative treatment of private property, and carries one weak Augustine tail chunk (score 0.38).

Ranking: hyde_haiku and hyde_cohere_luna are close, with hyde_haiku ahead on completeness and angle coverage and hyde_cohere_luna ahead on precision and redundancy; hyde_cohere_haiku trails both clearly.
