retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query is a pastoral cry of doubt/loss of faith. Strong hits: Augustine Confessions VI.4–5 (his own doubt and the reasonableness of believing what is not demonstrated), Hermas on putting away doubting, CCC §162 on perseverance in faith and the possibility of losing it, Theophilus's 'I used to disbelieve but now I believe,' Lumen Fidei §56, Summa II-II Q.2 on the act of faith (including whether reasons lessen merit — directly relevant to intellectual doubt). Psalms 42 and 77 ('Where is your God?', 'My soul refused to be comforted') are genuine biblical laments of felt absence of God — legitimately on-target for the experiential dimension of doubt rather than metaphorical filler. CCC §163–165 on faith as beginning of eternal life is somewhat adjacent (it does treat faith amid darkness, but the chunk shown is about the beatific vision), and Deus Caritas Est §38 and Lumen Fidei §57 pivot to suffering rather than unbelief — thematically neighboring but slightly off the specific concept. Sirach 2 is about temptation/testing in serving the Lord, close enough. No wrong-doctrine collision (nothing about, e.g., heresy penalties or a different doctrine sharing the word 'faith' such as justification by faith), but there are 3–4 chunks that drift toward the suffering/consolation theme rather than doubt about belief itself.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection: Catechism — it found §162 (perseverance in faith, losing faith) which is a strong canonical passage for this question, but missed §160 (freedom of faith) and the §176–184 summary that other pipelines surfaced; §163–165 is mid-tier for doubt. Confessions — Book VI ch. IV–V is precisely Augustine's canonical doubt narrative, excellent. Summa — Q.2 A.5 and A.10 on the act of faith; A.10 (whether reasons lessen merit of faith) is a good fit, A.5 less so, but the treatise on faith is the right locus. Scripture — Psalms 42 and 77 are the canonical laments of spiritual desolation, and 2 Cor 4 is apt; however Hebrews 10 ('do not throw away your confidence... do not shrink back') and Romans 8:35–39, arguably more canonical for holding on when belief wavers, are missing. Lumen Fidei — §§56–57 are about faith and suffering, not the encyclical's core treatment of faith's light and crisis of faith (§§3–5), so mid-tier. Overall a mix of canonical and mid-tier selections.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation, systematic/philosophical, magisterial/catechetical, pastoral application, historical precedent/witness. Scriptural: Psalms 42, 77, 2 Cor 4, Sirach 2 — strong. Systematic: two Summa articles on the act of faith. Magisterial/catechetical: CCC §162, §163–165; Lumen Fidei and Deus Caritas Est also function magisterially/pastorally. Historical witness: Augustine's Confessions, Theophilus, Hermas — patristic/autobiographical precedent. Pastoral: Lumen Fidei §57, Hermas's counsel to put away doubting. Four to five distinct angles are genuinely covered.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The tension in this topic: doubt is not identical with loss of faith / faith is a free gift that can be lost and must be nourished, versus reassurance that doubt is compatible with faith and God does not abandon the doubter; also faith's assent versus reason's role. The set has the 'faith can be shipwrecked, must persevere' pole (CCC §162), the 'believing what cannot be demonstrated is reasonable' pole (Augustine VI.5, Summa A.10), the experiential lament pole (Psalms 42/77, Deus Caritas Est §38 on Job), and the consolation pole (2 Cor 4, Lumen Fidei). What is thinner is the explicitly reassuring/freedom-of-faith and gratuity/gift-of-grace-restoration side that CCC §160 and §153–155 supply, and no explicit statement that involuntary doubt is not sin. Still, both the exhortative and consoling poles are present.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: two CCC chunks (§162 perseverance vs §163–165 faith as beginning of eternal life) — distinct arguments; two Psalms (42 and 77) — both are laments of felt divine absence making a very similar substantive move, mild overlap though from different psalms within the same collection; two Summa Q.2 articles (A.5 explicit belief obligation vs A.10 reasons and merit) — distinct; two Lumen Fidei chunks (§56 faith and speech in suffering, §57 suffering as mediator of light) — noticeably overlapping in theme and argument (faith amid suffering). So roughly one clear overlapping pair plus one mild pair.

scores.summary: Broad, multi-angle set with excellent patristic witness (Augustine, Hermas, Theophilus) and the strongest scriptural lament coverage (Ps 42, 77), but it drifts partly into the suffering theme (two Lumen Fidei chunks, Deus Caritas Est) and misses the Catechism's freedom-of-faith and in-brief passages that the other pipelines found.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Nearly every chunk engages doubt, belief, and perseverance directly: Augustine VI.4–5 (the canonical doubt narrative), Hermas on doubting, CCC §160 (faith must be free — directly answers 'what if I can't assent?'), CCC §162 (faith can be lost, must be nourished), Lumen Fidei §4 (the flame of faith dying out — precisely the query's situation) and §5 ('that your faith may not fail'), Theophilus's conversion from disbelief, Hebrews 10 (do not shrink back, hold fast the confession), Romans 8:35–39 and Romans 5:1–5 (nothing separates us; suffering produces hope) — reassurance rather than doubt per se but pastorally apposite, Summa I Q.2 A.2 (reason's preambles to faith — squarely relevant to intellectual doubt) and II-II Q.2 A.3 (belief above natural reason). Dilexit Nos §26 on faith becoming affection is somewhat adjacent, and Deus Caritas Est §38 (Job/suffering) and 2 Cor 4 lean toward the suffering theme. No wrong-doctrine collision; only mild drift in two or three chunks.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Catechism: found both §160 (freedom of faith) and §162 (perseverance/losing faith) — these are the two most canonical CCC passages for this question. Confessions: the top-ranked VI.4 and VI.5, the core doubt passages. Lumen Fidei: §§4–5, the encyclical's own framing of faith's flame dying out and Christ's prayer that faith not fail — much closer to the canonical treatment than the suffering sections. Summa: I Q.2 A.2 on demonstrability of God's existence plus II-II Q.2 A.3 on believing above reason — good loci, though II-II Q.2 A.10 (reasons and merit of faith) or Q.10 on unbelief would be even more targeted. Scripture: Hebrews 10 ('do not throw away your confidence'), Romans 8, Romans 5 — strong canonical choices for perseverance. Overall consistently high-tier selections across collections.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Scriptural: Romans 8, Romans 5, Hebrews 10, 2 Cor 4. Systematic/philosophical: two Summa articles on the relation of reason and faith. Catechetical/magisterial: CCC §160, §162. Pastoral/papal: Lumen Fidei §§4–5, Deus Caritas Est §38, Dilexit Nos §26. Historical witness: Augustine, Theophilus, Hermas. Five distinct applicable angles are all substantively represented.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: Both poles are well captured: the obligation/warning pole (CCC §162 shipwreck of faith, Hebrews 10 on shrinking back, Theophilus's call not to be sceptical) and the consoling/permissive pole (CCC §160 that faith must be free and cannot be coerced, Augustine's honest doubt, Lumen Fidei §5 Christ prays that faith may not fail, Romans 8 nothing can separate us, Deus Caritas Est on Job's legitimate complaint). It also holds the reason/faith tension from both sides: reason offers preambles (Summa I Q.2 A.2) yet faith exceeds natural reason (II-II Q.2 A.3). This is a genuinely balanced picture.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: two CCC chunks (§160 freedom vs §162 perseverance) — clearly distinct arguments; two Lumen Fidei chunks (§4 faith as light dimming vs §5 Christ's prayer/Year of Faith) — related but making different points, mild overlap; two Summa chunks (I Q.2 A.2 vs II-II Q.2 A.3) — both concern the reason/faith boundary and are adjacent in substance, though one is about demonstrating God's existence and the other about the necessity of supernatural belief; two Romans passages (5 and 8) — both consolation-in-affliction but distinct arguments (hope from endurance vs inseparability from Christ's love); two Augustine chapters — consecutive and continuous narrative, some overlap but complementary stages of his doubt. Overall mostly distinct with a couple of mild overlaps, no wasted slots.

scores.summary: The most tightly targeted set: it lands the two key Catechism passages (freedom of faith and perseverance), Lumen Fidei's own account of faith's flame dimming, Augustine's doubt narrative, and both sides of the reason/faith relation, spanning all five applicable angles with little redundancy.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Top results are all squarely on doubt and the nature of belief: Augustine VI.4–5, Hermas on doubting, CCC §160 (freedom of faith), CCC §176–184 (In Brief on what faith is — relevant to what one is being asked to believe), Lumen Fidei §4 (flame of faith dying out) and §5 (that your faith may not fail), Clement of Alexandria Stromata II.6 on faith versus supposition and the philosophers (directly engages whether faith is rationally credible), Summa II-II Q.2 A.10 (whether supporting reasons lessen faith's merit) and I Q.2 A.2 (preambles to faith), Hebrews 10 (do not shrink back), 1 Peter 1:3–12 (faith tested by fire, living hope). Slight drift: Deus Caritas Est §38 and 2 Cor 4 toward suffering; Dilexit Nos §26 toward affective faith; Romans 8:35–39 is consolation rather than doubt. No wrong-doctrine collision.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Catechism: §160 (freedom of faith) is canonical for this question; §176–184 is the In Brief summary — useful but a compendium rather than the targeted treatment, and notably CCC §162 on perseverance/losing faith (found by the other two pipelines) is absent, which is arguably the single most on-point CCC passage. Confessions: VI.4 and VI.5, the canonical doubt chapters, ranked first. Lumen Fidei: §§4–5, the encyclical's framing of the dying flame and Christ's prayer for Peter's faith — high-tier. Summa: II-II Q.2 A.10 on reasons and merit of faith is an excellent fit, plus I Q.2 A.2. Patristic: Clement Stromata II.6 is a substantive treatment of faith versus opinion. Scripture: Hebrews 10 and 1 Peter 1 (faith tested by fire) are strong; Romans 8 is fine. Very good overall, with the one notable Catechism gap.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Scriptural: Hebrews 10, 1 Peter 1, Romans 8, 2 Cor 4. Systematic/philosophical: two Summa articles plus Clement's philosophical defense of faith as more than supposition. Catechetical: CCC §160 and the In Brief §176–184. Pastoral/papal: Lumen Fidei §§4–5, Dilexit Nos §26, Deus Caritas Est §38. Historical witness: Augustine, Hermas, Clement. All five applicable angles are represented, with unusually strong philosophical coverage.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The consoling/permissive pole is strong: faith must be free and uncoerced (CCC §160), Augustine's honest doubt vindicated, Christ prays that faith may not fail (LF §5), nothing separates us (Rom 8), faith tested by fire yields praise (1 Pet 1). The definitional pole is present (CCC In Brief on assent of intellect and will; Clement and Aquinas on faith's rational standing). The exhortative/warning pole is thinner: Hebrews 10's 'do not shrink back' carries it, but CCC §162 on faith being losable and needing to be nourished by the word and works of charity is absent, so the responsibility-to-persevere side is somewhat underweighted relative to the reassurance side.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: two CCC chunks (§160 freedom vs §176–184 In Brief) — the In Brief partly restates definitional material, mild overlap; two Lumen Fidei chunks (§4 and §5) — related but distinct points; two Summa chunks (II-II Q.2 A.10 and I Q.2 A.2) — both bear on reason's relation to belief, adjacent but distinct arguments; two Augustine chapters — consecutive narrative, complementary; multiple Scripture passages from different books, not redundant. No pair is a straight restatement; a couple of mild overlaps.

scores.summary: Strong, doubt-focused set with the best philosophical depth (Clement plus two Summa articles on faith and reason) and the canonical Augustine and CCC §160 passages, but it omits CCC §162 on perseverance and losing faith, leaving the exhortative pole slightly thin, and its CCC In Brief chunk is a compendium rather than a targeted treatment.

judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines share a solid core (Augustine's Confessions VI.4–5, Hermas on doubting, Deus Caritas Est §38, 2 Cor 4) and none commits a vocabulary collision — an easy failure here would have been retrieving passages on heresy, apostasy penalties, or 'justification by faith' as a different doctrine, and none did.

hyde_haiku is the widest-ranging and has the best scriptural lament coverage (Psalms 42 and 77 capture the felt absence of God better than anything the others retrieved), but it spends the most slots drifting into the adjacent theme of suffering (two Lumen Fidei chunks on faith-and-suffering, plus Deus Caritas Est and Sirach 2), and it misses CCC §160 on the freedom of faith, which directly addresses a person unable to assent.

hyde_cohere_haiku is the most precisely targeted: it uniquely captures BOTH key Catechism passages (§160 freedom of faith and §162 perseverance/shipwreck), pairs them with Lumen Fidei's own account of the flame of faith dying out, and holds both sides of the reason/faith relation from the Summa. Its doctrinal balance between warning and reassurance is the strongest of the three.

hyde_cohere_luna has the deepest philosophical layer (Clement's Stromata on faith versus supposition alongside two Summa articles) and the highest-confidence ranking of the Augustine doubt chapters, plus 1 Peter's 'faith tested by fire.' Its weakness is the absence of CCC §162, replaced by the In Brief compendium, which leaves the perseverance/losable-faith pole underrepresented.

Overall: hyde_cohere_haiku edges ahead on best-passage selection and doctrinal completeness; hyde_cohere_luna is very close with better philosophical breadth; hyde_haiku trails slightly on relevance precision and redundancy.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Top chunks are squarely on target: CCC §971 (devotion to Mary), ST III q25 a5 (whether Mary should receive latria — the exact worship/veneration distinction), ST II-II q83 a4 (whether we ought to pray to God alone — directly the intercession question), CCC §2673-2679 (prayer in communion with Mary), Redemptoris Mater §38 (one mediator vs. Marian mediation), Mediator Dei §168-169 (invoking saints and Mary). Scripture chunks (Cana, Magnificat, Visitation) are legitimate scriptural foundation for Marian intercession and honor ('all generations will call me blessed'). Augustine on idolatry/latria vs. dulia is relevant to the worship objection. Origen Against Celsus V.11 and VIII.9, however, concern worship of the sun/rational light and pagan worship of created things in an anti-Celsus polemic — these are vocabulary collisions on 'worship' with no bearing on Marian veneration. The Ignatius Epistle to Hero chunk ('do not hold women in abomination... love those that were the authors of our birth') is entirely off-topic — a pastoral exhortation to a deacon, retrieved on 'mother/woman' vocabulary. That is a clear off-doctrine intrusion. Three tail chunks are essentially noise.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection: Catechism — found §971 (Devotion to the Blessed Virgin) and §2673-2679 (In communion with the holy Mother of God); these are the canonical passages, though CCC §2110-2132 (latria/idolatry) or §487-507 would add more. hyde_haiku has the best doctrinal breadth on the sharing pole — Populorum Progressio §23 (Ambrose's 'you are not making a gift of your possessions') and Centesimus Annus §31 on the origin of goods and labor as a title are genuinely valuable additions no other pipeline finds — but it is the only pipeline that misses Rerum Novarum §8 entirely, and its tail is the weakest, with Irenaeus on the despoiling of the Egyptians, Luke 12:22–34 on anxiety, and Sirach 14 on stinginess occupying slots.

[3] ST q32 a5 ad2 on superfluous goods belonging to the needy is the opposite pole. [4] QA §50 on superfluous income, [5] Mater et Magistra §121, [7] CCC 2402-2406 on private ownership plus universal destination, [8] Populorum Progressio §23, [10] CCC 2407 on temperance/moderation of attachment — all squarely on the concept. judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines correctly identify this as a question with two doctrinal poles — the legitimacy of private property and licit enjoyment of created goods versus the universal destination of goods and the obligation of superfluity — and all three retrieve from the same five-angle spread (Scripture, Summa, Catechism, social encyclicals, Fathers), so multi-angle coverage is uniformly excellent and not a differentiator.

The differentiators are passage precision and redundancy. hyde_cohere_luna has the best individual passages: it alone pairs both decisive Summa articles (q32 a6 on giving out of what one needs, q117 a1 ad2 on not impoverishing oneself) with 1 Tim 6:17-19 and the full encyclical set. But it squanders three of sixteen slots on Matthew, Mark, and Luke telling the same rich-ruler story, plus two overlapping Cyprian treatises, making it the most redundant set.

Its cost is one genuinely off-target chunk — Augustine, City of God I.10, on the saints losing nothing when temporal goods are taken — which is a providence/theodicy passage pulled in on 'temporal goods' vocabulary, and it misses 1 Tim 6:17-19.

hyde_cohere_haiku sits between them: strong balance and the best-ranked scriptural passage, no off-topic chunk, but it misses both ST q32 a6 and Rerum Novarum §22 and wastes slots on a bare Cyprian proof-text list and a duplicated synoptic pericope.

Net: hyde_haiku offers the most useful overall answer set despite one relevance lapse; hyde_cohere_luna has the best passages but the worst slot economy; hyde_cohere_haiku is the safest but least precise.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query asks why God commands the sacrifice of Isaac — i.e., the purpose of the testing, its meaning in salvation history, and how it can be commanded at all. Chunk [1] Cyprian Testimony XV ('men are tried by God... that they may be proved') quotes Gen 22 directly and states the purpose of the trial — dead-on. [3] and [5] Augustine City of God XVI.32 explicitly treat Abraham's obedience proved by the offering of Isaac, including exegesis of 'now I know.' [4] Genesis 22 is the primary text. [6] Summa II-II q.97 a.1 on the temptation/testing of God is adjacent — it treats humans tempting God rather than God testing humans, so it's a partial vocabulary overlap on 'tempt,' though the article's discussion of testing does illuminate the notion. [9] Summa q.104 a.4 'whether God ought to be obeyed in all things' bears directly on the Abraham command problem. [11] Augustine's Doctrinal Treatises III.11 is about whether an angel or God spoke — a peripheral concern of the same pericope, on-passage but off-question. [2], [10] Lumen Fidei §§10–11 concern Abraham's faith in God's word broadly, thematically related but not focused on the Aqedah. [7] CCC 144–149 explicitly names Abraham's obedience of faith and typically covers the sacrifice of Isaac. [12] CCC 2570–2573 covers Abraham's prayer and includes the Moriah episode. No chunk belongs to an entirely different doctrine; the weakest ones ([6], [11]) are adjacent within the same textual field rather than true doctrinal collisions.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Genesis: Gen 22:1–19 is exactly the canonical passage. Augustine City of God: XVI.32 is the canonical chapter, and both the framing and the 'now I know' exegesis were retrieved — excellent. Catechism: CCC 144–149 (obedience of faith, where the Church treats Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac) and 2570–2573 (which contains the Moriah/prefigurement material) are both strong, close to canonical. Hebrews 11:8–19 is the canonical NT interpretation, including the resurrection-faith reasoning about Isaac. Summa: q.104 a.4 is the right locus for how God can command such an act, though the pipeline got only the Reply to Obj. 2 rather than the objection stating the Abraham problem; q.97 a.1 is a mid-tier pick. Cyprian's Testimony XV is precisely the 'trial to prove' heading. Lumen Fidei §§10–11 are about Abraham's faith generally; the encyclical's more directly relevant passage on the sacrifice of Isaac (LF §12 area) was not caught. Augustine's Doctrinal Treatises III.11 is a peripheral mention. Overall a strong majority of collections represented by their core or near-core treatments.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation, patristic/historical precedent, systematic/philosophical reasoning, magisterial/catechetical teaching, and pastoral/spiritual application. Scriptural: Genesis 22 and Hebrews 11. Patristic/historical: Cyprian, Augustine (two works). Systematic: two Summa articles on testing and on obedience to divine commands, including the moral-philosophical problem. Magisterial/catechetical: CCC twice plus Lumen Fidei. Pastoral/spiritual: CCC 2570–2573 on prayer and Lumen Fidei's application to the believer's journey. Four to five distinct angles are genuinely present.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The doctrinal tension here is real: God appears to command something intrinsically evil (killing an innocent), and Scripture says God 'tempted' Abraham though God tempts no one. The pipeline captures the affirmation side well (test of faith and obedience, Abraham as model). It also captures the resolving nuance: Augustine's exegesis that 'now I know' means 'I made known,' not that God learned; Summa q.104 a.4 Reply to Obj. 2 explaining that God's command does not contravene virtue since God is the author of life and dominion; Cyprian on trial as proof, not seduction. What is thinner is the typological/Christological pole — Isaac as figure of Christ and the ram/substitution pointing to the Father's offering of the Son — present only implicitly via Hebrews 11 and possibly CCC 2572. Also absent is the anti-child-sacrifice dimension (the episode as repudiation of human sacrifice). Both main poles are represented; some depth missing.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Two Augustine City of God XVI.32 chunks appear, but they are sequential and substantively distinct — one gives the framing of the trial and Abraham's piety, the other the exegetical resolution of 'now I know' and what follows. Two Lumen Fidei chunks (§10, §11) overlap noticeably: both argue that Abraham entrusts himself to God's word and that this word grounds his journey; §11 adds the recognition of a call already at his core, so overlap is partial. Two Summa chunks come from different questions (q.97 and q.104) with different arguments. Two CCC chunks address obedience of faith and prayer respectively — distinct. Only one same-source pair shows meaningful argumentative overlap.

scores.summary: A strong, well-balanced result set: canonical Genesis 22 plus Hebrews, the core Augustine chapter in two complementary segments, Cyprian's on-point testimony heading, two Summa articles engaging the moral problem, and catechetical/magisterial material. Weaknesses are the adjacent Summa q.97 on tempting God, the peripheral Augustine angel-identity chunk, and mild Lumen Fidei overlap; the Christological typology is only implicit.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Core chunks are excellent: Genesis 22 (primary text), Augustine City of God XVI.32 twice (the canonical patristic treatment of why Abraham was tested), CCC 144–149 and 2570–2573, Hebrews 11:8–19, and Summa q.104 a.4 on obeying God's commands. But this set adds several chunks that share only vocabulary or characters. [8] Irenaeus Against Heresies IV.5 §25 is about Christ being the God of the living who spoke to the fathers — a Christological/anti-Marcionite argument that mentions the patriarchs; it does not address the testing of Abraham. [9] Clement of Rome ch. X concerns Abraham's obedience in leaving his country and the promise, not the sacrifice of Isaac. [10] Summa q.85 a.1 on whether sacrifice is of the natural law is a different doctrine — the general theology of cultic sacrifice — retrieved on the keyword 'sacrifice' and 'Isaac offered sacrifice'; this is a genuine vocabulary collision with the query's 'sacrifice.' multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Scriptural: Psalm 22, Isaiah 53, Matthew 27, Mark 15. Systematic/philosophical: Summa q.50 a.2 (twice) on the Godhead's separation from the flesh. Magisterial: CCC §602–603, §612, Redemptor Hominis §9, Dives in Misericordia §8, Deus Caritas Est §38. redundancy_rate.reasoning: The clearest problem is two chunks from the very same Summa article — q.50 a.2 Objection 1 and its Reply. scores.summary: The strongest soteriological coverage of the three — it uniquely finds CCC §602–603 ('made him to be sin'), Isaiah 53, Redemptor Hominis §9, and the anti-Arian Alexander of Alexandria, spanning five angles. retrieval_relevance.reasoning: This set is the most conceptually focused on the actual question — how the cry squares with divinity. The weak tail: Deus Caritas Est §38 (Job's complaint — theodicy, adjacent vocabulary of crying out to God) and Dives in Misericordia §7 (general Paschal-mystery mercy). best_passage_selection.reasoning: Summa: both canonical articles — q.50 a.2 on whether the Godhead was separated from the flesh at death (with the reply directly glossing 'forsaken') and q.46 a.12 on attributing the Passion to the Godhead. Divinity/unbroken union: ST q.50 a.2 (the forsaking does not dissolve the personal union), ST q.46 a.12 (the Passion belongs to the Godhead only via the human nature it assumed), Philippians 2 ('existing in the form of God'), Dionysius ('nevertheless He was not forsaken'). True humanity/real anguish: CCC §470 on the full reality of the human soul with its own operations of intellect and will, Hebrews 2, Justin on Christ 'truly become man capable of suffering,' Dilexit Nos §60/§62 explicitly against those who downplayed Christ's human affections, Philippians 2's self-emptying. scores.summary: The most precisely targeted set for the question as posed: it pairs both canonical Summa articles on whether the Passion touches the Godhead with CCC §470 on the two natures and with Philippians 2 and Hebrews 2, then adds the patristic Psalm-22 exegesis and Dilexit Nos on Christ's real human affections — giving the cleanest both-poles picture across all five angles. judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines share a solid core (ST III q.50 a.2 on whether the Godhead separated from the flesh, Psalm 22, Mark 15, CCC §612, Justin XCIX, Dionysius II, Deus Caritas Est §38) and all three cover the full range of applicable angles — scriptural, systematic, magisterial, patristic/historical, and pastoral — so multi-angle coverage does not discriminate between them.

They diverge on which side of the doctrinal problem they illuminate. hyde_cohere_haiku is the most precisely aligned with the query's actual hinge ('if he is divine'): it retrieves both canonical Summa articles, CCC §470 on the full reality of Christ's human soul in the hypostatic union, and Philippians 2's kenosis plus Hebrews 2 — the classic dogmatic scriptures for the divinity/humanity tension — and Dilexit Nos §60/§62 on the reality of Christ's human affections. Its main gap is soteriological: nothing on Christ bearing our sin.

hyde_haiku inverts this. It uniquely finds CCC §602–603 ('for our sake God made him to be sin'), Isaiah 53, Redemptor Hominis §9 and Alexander of Alexandria's anti-Arian epistle, giving the best account of why Christ voices dereliction as our representative — but it never retrieves an explicit two-natures/hypostatic-union passage, spends two slots on the objection and reply of a single Summa article and two on the same Dionysius fragment, and includes a peripheral Dilexit Nos §45 on Jesus weeping over Jerusalem.

hyde_cohere_luna sits between the two, closely resembling hyde_cohere_haiku (both Summa articles, CCC §470, Justin XCVIII/XCIX, Dionysius II/III, Dilexit Nos §60/§62) but substituting Matthew 27 for Philippians 2 and carrying a slightly weaker tail, so its relevance is marginally more diluted and its dogmatic scripture slightly less apt.

On redundancy all three are penalized for same-source overlap: the Dionysius II/III pair and the Dilexit Nos §60/§62 pair in the two cohere variants, and in hyde_haiku the doubled single Summa article plus doubled Dionysius fragment, which is the heaviest duplication of the three.

XXIV, which is chiefly a polemical refutation of heretics on the Maker and the substance of the Lord — it shares the vocabulary of 'doctrines' and Church tradition but addresses heresy-refutation rather than the mechanism of development — and 2 Thess 2:13–17 / Ephesians 4:1–16, which are loosely apt (hold the traditions; unity and growth of the body) rather than squarely on doctrinal development. No outright wrong-doctrine collision, and the proportion of directly engaged chunks is higher than in the other runs.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Summa: the canonical q.1 a.7 article body plus a reply — the corpus's single best systematic treatment. Catechism: §94–95, the precise 'Growth in understanding the faith' section, plus §249–252 as a case study. Papal magisterium: Singulari Quidem §8 at top rank is the classic formulation; Veritatis Splendor §27 on living Tradition and Lumen Fidei §48 are apt sections; but as with the sibling pipeline, Ut Unum Sint §18–19 and Evangelii Gaudium §41 — the passages that most directly state that the deposit is unchanged while its expression develops — were not retrieved. Patristics: Origen's Preface is close to the canonical early text; Irenaeus is represented three times, of which Book I ch. X (rule of faith) is the strongest and Book III ch. XXIV is a peripheral polemical passage. Scripture is represented only by mid-tier passages. Strong central selections with one meaningful magisterial gap.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural, systematic, magisterial, historical precedent, pastoral. Systematic: Summa q.1 a.7. Magisterial/papal: Singulari Quidem, Veritatis Splendor, Lumen Fidei, Evangelii Gaudium, CCC. Historical precedent: Origen, three Irenaeus passages, formation of Trinitarian dogma. Scriptural: 2 Thess and Ephesians. Pastoral: Evangelii Gaudium §40 on theologians helping the Church's judgment mature. Three-plus distinct applicable angles are covered substantively, though the scriptural angle is thin and represented only by loosely related texts.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: Both poles appear: growth in understanding (CCC §94–95, Summa, Evangelii Gaudium §40, Origen) and the unchangeability of the deposit and of dogmatic meaning (Singulari Quidem §8 explicitly, Lumen Fidei §48 on integrity of articles, Irenaeus's rule of faith preserved everywhere identically, Irenaeus III.24 on the Church guarding truth against novelty). Veritatis Splendor §27 gives the magisterial safeguard. Missing is the explicit modern criterion for distinguishing development of formulation from change of meaning (Ut Unum Sint §18, Evangelii Gaudium §41), which would sharpen the answer, but the substantive tension is genuinely represented on both sides.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: The two Summa chunks are from the same article but carry different arguments (implicit-in-explicit articles vs. progress on the part of the learner). Three Irenaeus chunks are from three different books: Book I ch. X (rule of faith), Book IV ch. IX (new and old treasure), Book III ch. XXIV (refutation of heretics and the Church's preservation of truth) — related in theme but Book III and Book I both effectively assert the Church's uniform preservation of apostolic faith, a partial overlap in substantive point and the weakest of the three adds little. Two CCC chunks are distinct. So one same-source pair overlaps modestly; the rest is varied.

scores.summary: The tightest of the three sets: it keeps every high-value chunk, elevates Singulari Quidem §8 to first rank, and drops the weakest keyword-driven scriptural filler, at the cost of a somewhat redundant third Irenaeus passage and a thin scriptural angle.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: This set uniquely surfaces the passages that answer the question most exactly: Ut Unum Sint §18 ('not a question of altering the deposit of faith, changing the meaning of dogmas') and §19 (doctrine must be presented understandably), Evangelii Gaudium §41 ('the deposit of the faith is one thing, the way it is expressed is another'), and Veritatis Splendor §1 quoting John XXIII's identical formula. Together with Summa q.1 a.7 and CCC §94–95 these engage the precise mechanism of development-without-change. Tertullian on truth progressive in its developments is thematically apt. CCC §249–252 is a legitimate case history. Weak spots: Irenaeus Book II ch. XXVIII is about the limits of human knowledge of creation and reserving some knowledge to God — related to epistemic humility but not to doctrinal development; 2 Corinthians 3:1–18 (letter vs. Spirit, the old and new covenants) shares 'letter/Spirit' language and could be read as a metaphor but does not address doctrinal development; Hebrews 6:1–12 ('leaving the first principles, press on to perfection') is a plausible scriptural analogue for growth; Ephesians 4:1–16 is loosely apt. So roughly three of fifteen chunks are matched on theme-adjacent vocabulary rather than the concept, but none is a distinct competing doctrine.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: This is the strongest run on canonical passages. Summa: q.1 a.7, the definitive article. Catechism: §94–95, the exact 'Growth in understanding the faith' section. Papal magisterium: Ut Unum Sint §18–19 and Evangelii Gaudium §41 and Veritatis Splendor §1 are precisely the loci where recent magisterium states that the deposit is unchanged while its formulation develops — these are the canonical modern answer passages the other two pipelines missed entirely. Patristics: Tertullian's chapter on truth progressive in its developments is apt; Irenaeus Book I ch. X (rule of faith) is the right immutability passage, but Book II ch. XXVIII is peripheral, and Origen's Preface — a stronger patristic locus — is absent here. Scripture: only mid-tier or peripheral selections. Averaged, this pipeline finds the canonical answer passage in most relevant collections.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural, systematic, magisterial, historical precedent, pastoral. Systematic: Summa q.1 a.7 (two segments) and Irenaeus II.28 on the limits of knowledge. Magisterial: Ut Unum Sint, Evangelii Gaudium, Veritatis Splendor, CCC — heavily covered. Pastoral: Ut Unum Sint §19 and Evangelii Gaudium §41 on presenting doctrine intelligibly in changing cultures is a genuine pastoral-application angle, better represented here than in the other runs. Historical precedent: Tertullian, Irenaeus, the Cyril and Methodius example, formation of Trinitarian dogma. Scriptural: Ephesians, 2 Corinthians 3, Hebrews 6. Four-plus distinct applicable angles.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: Both poles are captured with unusual precision. Affirmation of development: CCC §94–95, Summa q.1 a.7, Tertullian, Hebrews 6, Ut Unum Sint §19 on reformulating doctrine. Preservation pole: Ut Unum Sint §18 explicitly excludes altering the deposit, changing the meaning of dogmas, or eliminating essential words; Veritatis Splendor §1 insists the meaning is 'preserved intact'; Irenaeus's rule of faith holds the same faith everywhere. Evangelii Gaudium §41 states the distinction that resolves the tension. This is the most complete rendering of both poles of the three sets; if anything only an explicit conciliar citation of Dei Verbum §8 is missing.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Two same-source pairs raise concerns. Ut Unum Sint §18 and §19 are consecutive sections, but §18 argues the deposit is not altered while §19 argues doctrine must be expressed intelligibly — complementary, not restating. The clearer overlap is between Evangelii Gaudium §41 and Veritatis Splendor §1, which both quote John XXIII's 'deposit of faith is one thing, the manner of expression another' — but these are different sources, and cross-source convergence is a positive signal rather than redundancy. The two Summa segments from q.1 a.7 make different arguments; the two Irenaeus chunks are from different books on different matters; the two CCC chunks are distinct. Very little genuine same-source restatement.

scores.summary: The most doctrinally precise set: it alone retrieves the 'deposit of faith is one thing, its expression another' passages from Ut Unum Sint, Evangelii Gaudium and Veritatis Splendor that directly resolve the question, with strong pastoral and magisterial coverage; it loses a little to a peripheral Irenaeus chunk, the absence of Origen, and a soft 2 Corinthians 3 match.

judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines share a strong spine: Summa II-II q.1 a.7 (the canonical systematic article on whether the articles of faith increase over time), CCC §94–95 on growth in understanding the faith, CCC §249–252 as a dogmatic case history, and Irenaeus on the rule of faith and the new-and-old treasure. They differ decisively in the magisterial passages they surface and in the quality of their scriptural tails.

hyde_haiku is the most doctrinally on-target: it uniquely retrieves Ut Unum Sint §18–19, Evangelii Gaudium §41 and Veritatis Splendor §1 — the passages that state the very distinction the query turns on, namely that the deposit of faith and the meaning of dogmas are unchanged while their formulation develops. This gives it the best canonical-passage selection, the strongest pastoral-application angle, and the most complete treatment of both poles of the doctrine. Its costs are a peripheral Irenaeus II.28 chunk on the limits of knowledge, a soft 2 Corinthians 3 match, and the loss of Origen's Preface.

hyde_cohere_luna and hyde_cohere_haiku share an identical high-value core (Singulari Quidem §8, Veritatis Splendor §27, Evangelii Gaudium §40, Origen, Lumen Fidei §48) but both miss the deposit-versus-expression formulations. Between them, luna is cleaner: it trims the weakest keyword-driven scriptural chunks (1 Tim 1:3–11, 2 Tim 4:1–8) that hyde_cohere_haiku retains, and it promotes Singulari Quidem §8 to first rank. Its one drawback is a third Irenaeus passage (Book III ch. XXIV) that partly duplicates the immutability point already made by Book I ch. X.

Net: hyde_haiku wins on best-passage selection and doctrinal completeness; hyde_cohere_luna wins on precision of the overall result set; hyde_cohere_haiku is the weakest, diluted by four low-value Pauline pastoral chunks matched largely on the word 'doctrine.'

query: Do I have to forgive someone who has never apologized and may hurt me again?
rationale: forgiveness versus reconciliation, justice, and safety

top.reference: Augustine — Doctrinal Treatises of St. Augustin, Chapter 73

Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part (Second Part of the Second Part) (Qq. 1–189), Question 188 - Of the Different Kinds of Religious Life (EIGHT ARTICLES), Article 3 - Whether a religious order can be directed to soldiering?

Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part (Second Part of the Second Part) (Qq. 1–189), Question 25 - Of the Object of Charity (TWELVE ARTICLES), Article 9 - Whether it is necessary for salvation that we should show our enemies the  signs and effects of love?

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query is a pastoral/moral question: is forgiveness obligatory absent repentance, and does it require exposing oneself to further harm? Chunks 1 and 2 (Fratelli Tutti §250, §241) are precisely on point — forgiveness without forgetting, and forgiveness that does not require submitting to continued oppression. Matthew 18:21-35 (seventy times seven / unforgiving servant), Luke 17:1-4, Augustine ch. 73, Cyprian Testimony XXII, Dives in Misericordia §14, and Constitutions of the Holy Apostles all engage the duty to forgive directly. Summa II-II Q25 a.8 and a.9 on love of enemies and whether interior love must be shown outwardly are directly germane to the 'may hurt me again' aspect (distinguishing interior charity from external association). Luke 6 and Romans 12 on loving enemies / not repaying evil are adjacent but genuinely part of the same moral question. The weakest is CCC §1822-1829 on charity as a theological virtue — a general treatment of charity that is thematically related but not about forgiveness of an unrepentant offender; it is broad rather than a wrong-doctrine collision. No chunk addresses a different doctrine entirely (e.g. nothing about sacramental absolution or indulgences misfiring in). So no true vocabulary collision, but one generic filler.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection: Fratelli Tutti — §250 and §241 are the canonical passages on forgiveness without forgetting and forgiveness that does not mean submitting to injustice; excellent (though §251 on breaking the cycle of revenge, retrieved by hyde_haiku, is a close companion). Gospels — Matthew 18:21-35 (the seventy-times-seven pericope and unforgiving servant) is the single most canonical scriptural passage for this query, and it is found; Luke 17:1-4 and Luke 6 also on point. Summa — Q25 a.8 and a.9 are the core articles on love of enemies and outward signs of love, the correct systematic loci. Dives in Misericordia §14 is the central section on forgiveness and mercy in that encyclical. Augustine ch. 73 is the appropriate chapter, though ch. 74 (God does not pardon those who do not forgive from the heart) is arguably even more targeted and was missed. Catechism — §2839-2845 on 'forgive us our trespasses' is the right locus but the retrieved slice is the opening/generic part; §2838 (the astonishing petition) and the §2843 passage on forgiving from the heart / praying for the offender are the sharpest and were not fully captured; CCC §1822-1829 on charity is mid-tier. Overall canonical hits in most collections with a somewhat weak Catechism selection.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation, systematic/philosophical reasoning, magisterial/papal teaching, pastoral application, and patristic/historical precedent. Scriptural: Matthew 18, Luke 6, Luke 17, Romans 12. Systematic: Summa II-II Q25 a.8 and a.9. Magisterial/pastoral: Fratelli Tutti §§241, 250 and Dives in Misericordia §14; Catechism catechetical/pastoral treatment of the Our Father petition. Historical/patristic: Augustine, Cyprian, Constitutions of the Holy Apostles. All five applicable angles are represented with substance.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The genuine tension here is between the unconditional obligation to forgive from the heart and the legitimate limits — that forgiveness is not impunity, does not require forgetting, does not oblige one to renounce rights or remain exposed to an unrepentant abuser, and that reconciliation is distinct from forgiveness. The affirmative pole is heavily represented (Matthew 18, Augustine, Cyprian, Dives in Misericordia, Constitutions). The balancing pole is present and strong: Fratelli Tutti §241 explicitly says loving an oppressor does not mean letting him continue oppressing and does not require renouncing rights; §250 says forgiving is not forgetting; Summa Q25 a.9 distinguishes interior love owed to all from the outward signs owed only when circumstances permit — precisely the 'may hurt me again' nuance. Missing only the Fratelli Tutti §251 elaboration and any explicit treatment of justice/legitimate self-protection or the distinction between forgiveness and reconciliation in the Catechism. Both poles are genuinely captured.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Two chunks from Constitutions of the Holy Apostles Book II Sec. VI appear; they are related but make distinguishable points (the duty to forgive trespasses / seventy-times-seven vs. the requirement of reconciliation before prayer). Summa Q25 a.8 and a.9 are same-source but address different questions (whether charity requires loving enemies vs. whether outward signs are necessary) — genuinely complementary. Fratelli Tutti §250 and §241 make distinct arguments. Two CCC chunks are from different sections (charity vs. the Lord's Prayer petition). Luke 6 and Matthew 18 differ. Only the Constitutions pair shows partial overlap in the ambient theme of forgiving one's brother.

scores.summary: A strong, well-balanced result set: the canonical Matthew 18 pericope, the two decisive Fratelli Tutti paragraphs, and the correct Summa articles, spanning scripture, systematic theology, magisterium, and patristics, with both poles of the forgiveness/self-protection tension present. Weakest point is the generic CCC charity chunk and a somewhat mid-tier Lord's Prayer slice.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Fratelli Tutti §241 and §250 top the list and are exactly on point. Summa Q25 a.9, Luke 17:1-4, Luke 6, Romans 12, Sirach 28 (a superbly targeted wisdom text on forgiving the neighbor's hurt and not harboring anger), Dives in Misericordia §14, Augustine, Cyprian, and Constitutions all directly engage forgiving one who has wronged us. CCC §2302-2306 on peace, anger and vengeance is adjacent — it addresses the illicitness of revenge and desire for vengeance, which is relevant to the disposition of the wounded party, though its primary subject is the fifth commandment and peace/war rather than interpersonal forgiveness. The clearest problem is Summa Q188 a.3, 'Whether a religious order can be directed to soldiering?' — retrieved at rank 3 with 0.91. Its reply-to-objection happens to discuss not resisting evil and forgiving wrongs done to oneself, so it is not purely a vocabulary accident, but the passage's actual doctrinal subject is the licitness of military religious orders, an entirely different question; this is close to a vocabulary collision occupying a high-value slot. Notably, Matthew 18:21-35, the single most canonical passage, is absent.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Fratelli Tutti — §241 and §250, the canonical paragraphs, both found: excellent. Scripture — Luke 6, Luke 17, Romans 12 and Sirach 28 are all good, but the central and most obviously canonical passage, Matthew 18:21-35 (seventy times seven and the unforgiving servant), is missing, a significant gap for a query about repeated/unrepented offense. Summa — Q25 a.9 is a correct locus, but a.8 (whether charity requires loving enemies) is absent and instead the pipeline supplies Q188 a.3 on religious orders and soldiering, a peripheral place where the Summa merely brushes the theme; the corpus plainly has better Summa passages that were not found. Catechism — §2839-2845 slice retrieved is a mid-tier fragment about the Eucharist and reconciliation before the altar rather than the core treatment of the petition; §2302-2306 on peace is likewise tangential. Dives in Misericordia §14 and Augustine ch. 73 are appropriate. Overall a mixed picture: strong magisterial selection, weakened Summa and scriptural selection.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Scriptural: Luke 6, Luke 17, Romans 12, Sirach 28 — including an Old Testament wisdom angle other pipelines lack. Systematic: Summa Q25 a.9 (and, weakly, Q188 a.3). Magisterial/pastoral: Fratelli Tutti §§241, 250; Dives in Misericordia §14; Catechism §2302-2306 and §2839-2845. Patristic/historical: Augustine, Cyprian, Constitutions of the Holy Apostles. Well over three distinct applicable angles are covered with substance.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The obligation-to-forgive pole is amply covered (Sirach 28, Luke, Augustine, Cyprian, Constitutions, Dives in Misericordia). The balancing pole is also present and in fact well served: Fratelli Tutti §241 on not renouncing rights or letting an oppressor continue, §250 on forgiveness not being forgetting, Summa Q25 a.9 distinguishing interior charity from outward signs, and CCC §2302-2306 on the licitness of proportionate redress versus vengeance, which adds a justice dimension. Both poles of the tension are represented; missing is any explicit distinction between forgiveness and reconciliation in the Catechism's own words.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Two Constitutions of the Holy Apostles chunks from the same section appear again, partially overlapping in the general duty-to-forgive theme though making somewhat different points (duty to forgive vs. reconcile before prayer). Two Summa chunks are from very different questions and are not redundant. Two CCC chunks are from distinct sections (peace/anger vs. Lord's Prayer). Fratelli Tutti §241 and §250 make distinct arguments. No pair essentially restates another; only the Constitutions pair is mildly wasteful.

scores.summary: Strong magisterial and scriptural breadth (including Sirach 28) with both doctrinal poles present, but the high-ranked Summa passage on military religious orders is close to a doctrinal misfire and the absence of Matthew 18:21-35 plus weak Catechism slices dent best-passage selection.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Every chunk engages forgiveness of an offender or the disposition toward one who has wronged us. CCC §2839-2845 and §2838 treat the Lord's Prayer petition and the requirement to forgive from the heart. Matthew 18:21-35 and Matthew 5:38-48 are the central Gospel texts; Luke 6 and Luke 17 likewise. Fratelli Tutti §241 and §251 address the limits of forgiveness and breaking the cycle of revenge. Summa Q25 a.8 and a.9 handle love of enemies and its outward expression. Augustine chs. 73 and 74 — the latter explicitly on God not pardoning those who do not forgive from the heart, and on the offender who asks forgiveness — are directly relevant. Dives in Misericordia §14, Constitutions, all on point. The only slightly off item is Dilexit Nos §187 on reparation, which concerns the offender's duty to acknowledge guilt and ask pardon rather than the victim's duty to forgive; it is a related facet of the reconciliation dynamic (and speaks to the 'never apologized' element from the other side), not a different doctrine. No vocabulary collision.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Catechism — this pipeline uniquely captures both §2838 (the 'astonishing petition') and the §2839-2845 core treatment, the canonical Catechism locus for this question. Gospels — Matthew 18:21-35 at rank 2 plus Matthew 5:38-48, Luke 6 and Luke 17: the strongest scriptural selection of the three. Summa — both Q25 a.8 and a.9, the correct systematic articles. Augustine — chs. 73 and 74, including the chapter most precisely about forgiving from the heart as a condition of divine pardon. Fratelli Tutti — §241 and §251 are on point, though §250 ('forgiving does not mean forgetting'), arguably the single best paragraph for the 'may hurt me again' worry, is absent, with §251 partly compensating. Dives in Misericordia §14 is the right section. Across collections this is consistently the canonical or near-canonical treatment.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Scriptural: Matthew 18, Matthew 5, Luke 6, Luke 17. Systematic: Summa Q25 a.8 and a.9. Magisterial/catechetical: CCC §2838, §2839-2845. Pastoral/papal: Fratelli Tutti §§241, 251; Dives in Misericordia §14; Dilexit Nos §187. Patristic/historical: Augustine chs. 73-74, Constitutions of the Holy Apostles. All five applicable angles are covered richly and distinctly.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The affirmative obligation is very thoroughly represented, including the sharp claim that God does not pardon those who do not forgive from the heart. The balancing pole is present but thinner than in the other pipelines: Fratelli Tutti §241 supplies the crucial qualification that loving an oppressor does not mean allowing continued oppression and does not require renouncing one's rights, and §251 that true forgiveness does not forget but refuses the cycle of revenge; Summa Q25 a.9 distinguishes interior love from the outward signs. However §250, the most explicit statement of forgiveness-without-forgetting and without excusing, is missing, and Matthew 5's 'turn the other cheek' plus Augustine's severity tilt the set toward the demanding pole. Dilexit Nos §187 actually reinforces that the offender owes acknowledgment of guilt, which indirectly supports the nuance. Both poles are there; the limiting pole is somewhat less prominent.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Several same-source pairs: two CCC chunks (§2838 and §2839-2845) are contiguous and both explicate the same petition, with meaningful overlap in argument that forgiveness is the condition of being forgiven; two Augustine chapters (73, 74) are adjacent and closely related, though 74 adds the distinct point about God withholding pardon; two Constitutions chunks from the same section partly overlap; two Summa articles are genuinely distinct; Matthew 5:38-48 and Luke 6:27-36 are parallel Synoptic pericopes making essentially the same 'love your enemies / turn the other cheek' argument, though from different books. The CCC pair and the Matthew/Luke parallel represent real slot waste, and this set has the highest overlap density of the three.

scores.summary: The deepest and most canonical selection — Matthew 18, both key CCC sections, both Summa articles, both Augustine chapters — with full multi-angle coverage; but it pays for that depth in redundancy (contiguous CCC sections, adjacent Augustine chapters, parallel Synoptic passages) and loses Fratelli Tutti §250, the sharpest statement of forgiveness's limits.

judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines converge on a strong core for this pastoral question — Fratelli Tutti §241, Dives in Misericordia §14, Summa II-II Q25, Luke 6/17, Augustine, Cyprian, and the Constitutions of the Holy Apostles — so differences lie in the unique tail.

hyde_haiku assembles the deepest doctrinal treatment: it alone secures both Catechism sections on the 'forgive us our trespasses' petition, both Summa articles on love of enemies, both relevant Augustine chapters, Matthew 18:21-35 at rank 2, and Fratelli Tutti §251. That depth costs it in redundancy (contiguous CCC sections, adjacent Augustine chapters, and the Matthew 5 / Luke 6 Synoptic parallel), and it misses Fratelli Tutti §250, the passage most directly answering the fear of renewed harm.

hyde_cohere_haiku is the best-balanced set: it holds both §250 and §241 at the top, retrieves Matthew 18, both Summa Q25 articles, and keeps redundancy low; its only real weakness is the generic CCC charity chunk and a mid-tier Lord's Prayer slice.

hyde_cohere_luna has excellent magisterial ranking and adds a distinctive Old Testament angle with Sirach 28, but it is the only pipeline to surface a substantively off-target passage in a high slot — Summa Q188 a.3 on whether a religious order may be directed to soldiering, retrieved at 0.91 — and it omits Matthew 18:21-35 entirely while offering weaker Catechism fragments. That combination makes it the least reliable of the three on relevance and best-passage selection, despite comparable breadth and doctrinal balance.

On doctrinal completeness all three do reasonably well, chiefly because Fratelli Tutti §241 (shared) supplies the essential qualification that forgiveness is not impunity and does not require remaining exposed to an oppressor; the pipelines that also carry §250 or §251 articulate that pole most clearly.

rationale: heresy, clarification, and conciliar authority

Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part (Second Part of the Second Part) (Qq. 1–189), Question 1 - Of Faith (Ten Articles), Article 10 - Whether it belongs to the Sovereign Pontiff to draw up a symbol of faith?

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query asks why ecumenical councils/creedal definitions were needed if the apostles already handed on the faith. The top results are squarely on point: ST II-II Q1 A10 ad 1 is the canonical scholastic answer (the apostolic truth was sufficient, but heretical perversion made explicit symbols necessary), A10 ad 2 addresses the power of subsequent councils to re-edit the symbol, Acts 15:1-6 and 15:22-29 give the Jerusalem Council as scriptural precedent, CCC 249-252 shows the historical development of Trinitarian dogma in response to error, Lumen Fidei 48 on the integrity of faith needing profession in each era, Origen's Preface on what the apostles left undefined for later inquiry — this is remarkably apt. CCC 888-892, Commissum Divinitus 4, Veritatis Splendor 27 supply the magisterial-authority rationale, which is adjacent but genuinely part of the answer. Weaker items: Veritatis Splendor 26 is about apostolic moral catechesis and specific rules of behavior — related to apostolic teaching but not to why councils were needed; Cyprian Ep. LXXI and LXXIV concern the baptism-of-heretics controversy and are conciliar-practice mentions rather than engagements with the question, though they do show councils in operation historically; Irenaeus III.24 is a concluding polemic against heretics, thematically adjacent (refuting error) but not addressing conciliar necessity. No outright wrong-doctrine collision, but several chunks drift into general magisterial-authority or anti-heresy vocabulary rather than the specific concept.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection: Summa — found the exact canonical article (Q1 A10, both replies), which is the corpus's single best treatment of why creeds/councils are needed beyond apostolic teaching; excellent. Scripture — Acts 15 is the canonical precedent, and both the debate section and the decree section are retrieved; excellent. Catechism — CCC 249-252 (formation of Trinitarian dogma) is a strong illustrative passage and CCC 888-892 the teaching office; however the most canonical Catechism passage for this query, CCC 94-95 on growth in understanding of the faith (and CCC 84-87 on the deposit of faith and magisterium), was missed — mid-to-good. Patristics — Origen's Preface on what the apostles left for later investigation is an outstanding find; Cyprian is peripheral (letters about a council's occasion rather than its rationale), and Irenaeus III.24 is a peripheral chapter compared to I.10 or III.3-4 on the rule of faith and succession. Papal documents — Lumen Fidei 48 is good though 49 (apostolic succession, transmission) is arguably better; Commissum Divinitus 4 is on-point for magisterial power. Overall a strong core with peripheral patristic selections.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation (Acts 15 Jerusalem Council), systematic/philosophical reasoning (Aquinas on the symbol of faith), magisterial/conciliar definition (CCC, Veritatis Splendor, Commissum Divinitus), historical precedent (Origen, Cyprian's councils, Irenaeus against heresies), and pastoral application (Lumen Fidei on professing faith in each era). All five are represented here: Acts 15 twice, ST Q1 A10 twice, CCC and encyclicals, and genuine early-church historical material. This is broad, multi-angle coverage well beyond three distinct angles.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The doctrinal tension here is between the completeness/sufficiency of the apostolic deposit (no new revelation after the apostles) and the legitimate development/explicitation of that deposit by councils. Both poles are present: ST A10 ad 1 explicitly states the truth of faith was already sufficiently explicit in Christ and the apostles (sufficiency pole) while explaining the need for explicit symbols against heresy (development pole); Origen states the apostles delivered certain points clearly while leaving other matters for later investigation — a textbook articulation of both poles; Lumen Fidei 48 addresses each era's need to profess faith integrally; CCC 249-252 illustrates dogma formed from what was always believed. query: Why should Christians trust Sacred Tradition? How is it different from merely human traditions?
rationale: apostolic Tradition versus changeable customs and traditions of men

LXXIII explicitly interrogates 'whence is that tradition?' — the exact divine-vs-human distinction the query asks; Irenaeus III.1 and III.4 on the apostles depositing truth in the Church. 2 Thess 2:15 (hold the traditions taught by word or letter) and 2 Thess 3:6 are canonical scriptural warrants; 2 Pet 1:16–21 ('not cunningly devised fables') supports the not-of-human-origin pole. retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query has two parts: grounds/purpose of excommunication, and whether it means damnation. The top results are squarely on target: Summa Suppl. Q21 A1 (definition of excommunication as separation from communion, and effect on prayers) and A2 (whether the Church should excommunicate — medicinal purpose), Mystici Corporis §23–24 (members who are excommunicated remain members / are still to be treated with charity — directly answers the damnation question), Matthew 18:15–20 (binding/loosing, treat as gentile), 1 Cor 5:1–5 and 5:9–13 (handing over to Satan 'that the spirit may be saved' — the classic medicinal-purpose text), CCC §1443–1445 on reconciliation with the Church. Cyprian Ep. LI and Matthew 18:10–14 supply the reconciliation/mercy pole and are relevant, if slightly indirect. Apostolic Constitutions Sec. V on the bishop's duty to judge and casting out is directly the penal-discipline angle. Etsi Multa §26 is an actual act of excommunication — a historical instance, relevant. Two weaker items: Quanto Conficiamur Moerore §8 is about extra ecclesiam nulla salus / invincible ignorance — adjacent (it does mention being stubbornly separated from unity, which bears on the damnation question), so it is topically connected rather than a collision. CCC §1446–1449 on the sacrament of Penance generally is thematically adjacent (restoration) but not about excommunication. Cyprian Ep. LXIII on lapsed idol-sacrificers and the altar is peripheral. The last Apostolic Constitutions chunk about bloodshed/murder is a partial vocabulary drift toward penal law generally ('cast him out') but still concerns exclusion from the congregation. No chunk is a clearly different doctrine masquerading via shared keywords; the weakest items are adjacent rather than collisions, though there is noticeable dilution in the tail.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Summa: found both Q21 A1 and A2, which is precisely the canonical scholastic treatment of the definition, congruity, and cause of excommunication — canonical hit. Mystici Corporis: §23–24, the passage explicitly addressing that excommunicates/sinners remain in the Body and are not to be despaired of — canonical for the damnation question. Scripture: Matt 18:15–20 and 1 Cor 5 (both segments) are the two canonical scriptural loci for ecclesial exclusion, including the 'that his spirit may be saved' clause. CCC: §1443–1445 on reconciliation with the Church is a good mid-to-high tier passage; the strictly canonical CCC material on excommunication (§1463 on reserved absolution of latae sententiae excommunication, and §1861 on not presuming damnation) is absent, and §1446–1449 is generic Penance. Patristic sources are represented by reasonable but not necessarily best passages (Cyprian LXIII is weak). Overall most relevant collections are represented by their strong or canonical passages, with the Catechism slightly under-served.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The doctrinal tension here is between excommunication as a real, grave penalty of exclusion from communion and its medicinal, non-damning character (it is not a judgment on eternal destiny; the Church cannot bind God's judgment; remission is always available). The punitive pole is well covered (Aquinas A2 on God's punishment, 1 Cor 5, Apostolic Constitutions on casting out, Etsi Multa as an actual censure, Quanto Conficiamur on separation from unity). The medicinal/hopeful pole is also present: 1 Cor 5:5 'that the spirit may be saved,' Mystici Corporis §24 on receiving the fallen with charity, §23 on members who are not necessarily predestined, Aquinas A2 explicitly framing punishment as ordered to drawing the sinner to good, CCC §1443–1445 on reintegration, Cyprian on mercy to the repentant, and the lost-sheep parable. Both poles are substantively represented. What is thin is an explicit statement that the Church never claims to know a person is damned (e.g., CCC §1861), but the reintegration and medicinal material substantially conveys it.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query has two parts: (a) why does the Church have binding/obligatory fasting rules, and (b) can an external practice help spiritually. ST II-II q.147 a.3 (two chunks) directly answers the authority-to-bind question; CCC 2041-2043 gives the precepts of the Church and their obligatory character; CCC 1430-1433 on interior penance directly addresses the external/interior relationship; Mediator Dei §24 and §35 address interior vs exterior worship and ascetic effort disposing one for grace — precisely the 'can externals help' question; Charitate Christi §14 explicitly on the precept of abstinence and fasting; Appetente Sacro §3 on the law of fasting and penance; Isaiah 58 is the classic scriptural critique of merely external fasting; Tertullian chapters trace the value of fasting before God. The three synoptic bridegroom passages (Mark 2, Luke 5, Matt 9) are near-duplicates of one another and only tangentially address the question — they concern the timing/appropriateness of fasting under Christ rather than the binding obligation or the spiritual efficacy of externals; still they are genuinely about fasting, not a different doctrine. No vocabulary collision (nothing about a different doctrine masquerading as fasting). The set is on-topic throughout, with a few loosely-relevant scriptural slots.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Summa: q.147 a.3 'Whether fasting is a matter of precept?' is exactly the canonical passage for the binding-obligation question, and both the corpus body and a Reply to Objection are retrieved — excellent. However, a.1 'Whether fasting is an act of virtue?' — the canonical answer to whether the external practice is spiritually beneficial — is missing, so the Summa side of the second half of the query is underserved. Catechism: 2041-2043 (precepts) and 1430-1433 (interior penance) are both core; 1434-1439 (many forms of penance: fasting/prayer/almsgiving) would have been the ideal complement and is absent. Mediator Dei §24 and §35 are strong, on-point sections on interior/exterior worship. Scripture: Isaiah 58 is the canonical text; Matthew 6:16-18 (the Lord's own teaching on how to fast) is a notable miss, replaced by three redundant synoptic bridegroom pericopes. Tertullian's On Fasting ch. III and IX are reasonable but ch. IX is a peripheral discussion of xerophagies. Overall: canonical hits on the binding-precept angle, mid-tier on the spiritual-efficacy angle.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation, systematic/philosophical reasoning, magisterial/papal teaching, pastoral application, historical/patristic precedent. Present: scriptural (Isaiah 58, Mark 2, Luke 5, Matt 9); systematic (Aquinas q.147 a.3 on ecclesiastical authority to bind); magisterial (CCC precepts, Mediator Dei, Charitate Christi, Appetente Sacro); pastoral (Appetente Sacro §3 and Charitate Christi §14 are directly pastoral exhortations to bishops on teaching the faithful); patristic/historical (Tertullian On Fasting, two chapters). All five applicable angles are represented — well above the three-angle threshold.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The doctrinal tension here is exactly between the binding, obligatory external discipline (positive ecclesiastical law) and the primacy of interior conversion (externals without interior penance are 'sterile and false'). Both poles are strongly present: Aquinas and CCC 2041-2043 plus Charitate Christi supply the obligation pole; CCC 1430-1433, Mediator Dei §24, Isaiah 58, and the bridegroom passages (fasting is relativized to Christ's presence) supply the interior-primacy/anti-formalism pole. Mediator Dei §35 supplies the synthesis: ascetic effort disposes one to receive grace better. A fuller picture might have included the positive theology of bodily discipline as sharing in Christ's cross, and the CCC's mitigation/dispensation nuance, but both poles of the central tension are genuinely represented.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Two chunks from Summa q.147 a.3 — but they are different segments (corpus on ecclesiastical authority vs. Reply to Obj. 3 on Augustine and universal custom), making distinct points, so only mild overlap. Two Mediator Dei chunks (§24, §35) make related but distinct arguments (interior primacy vs. asceticism disposing for the sacraments). The real problem is three near-identical synoptic parallels — Mark 2:18-20, Luke 5:33-35, Matthew 9:14-15 — the same pericope, the same substantive point, occupying three of fourteen slots. Although technically three different books, these are the same Gospel passage restated and constitute wasted slots rather than convergence across the tradition.

scores.summary: Strong, well-rounded set that nails the binding-precept question via Aquinas q.147 a.3 and CCC 2041-2043 while balancing it with interior-penance and Mediator Dei material; five angles covered and both doctrinal poles present. Weakened by three duplicate synoptic bridegroom passages and by missing Aquinas a.1 / Matthew 6:16-18 on the spiritual value of fasting itself.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Nearly every chunk engages the query directly. ST q.147 a.1 answers whether fasting is an act of virtue (the 'can an external practice help spiritually' half) and a.3 Reply to Obj. 1 answers the binding-precept half with unusual precision ('not binding absolutely, but binding on each who needs such a remedy'). Matthew 6:16-18 is Christ's own teaching on fasting; Isaiah 58 arrives via Justin Martyr's citation; Colossians 2:16-23 is the key Pauline caution against dietary regulations and self-abasement — directly relevant to whether external practices avail. Mediator Dei §31 and §157, Appetente Sacro Preamble and §3, Tertullian III and VI, Hermas Similitude V (true fasting and its reward) all engage fasting/penance. The weakest link is Hebrews 12:4-13 on divine chastening and discipline — thematically adjacent (discipline, training) but about God's paternal correction of the suffering believer rather than the Church's fasting discipline or the efficacy of external practice; this is a mild vocabulary/thematic slide on 'discipline' rather than a full wrong-doctrine collision. judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines converge on the two strongest anchors — Dilexit Nos §159, which explicitly names the distinction between healing compunction and discouraged, obsessive guilt, and 2 Corinthians 7, the scriptural locus of godly versus worldly sorrow — so the differentiation lies in what each adds around them.

hyde_cohere_haiku produced the cleanest set: it is the only pipeline to pair CCC §1790–1794 (Erroneous Judgment) with Veritatis Splendor §62 (conscience can be mistaken), the two most directly applicable magisterial texts, and it adds CCC §1783–1785 on formation of conscience as the practical remedy. It also avoided the diluting chunks (Romans 14, Augustine) that appeared elsewhere. Its weaknesses are internal duplication — two Summa articles making essentially the same Aristotelian argument that sorrow for sin admits of a virtuous mean — and the narrowest angle spread, with one scriptural chunk and no patristic source.

hyde_cohere_luna is nearly as strong on relevance and clearly the broadest: five distinct angles, two well-chosen and non-overlapping Summa articles (erroneous conscience in confession, and moderation of penitential sorrow), both major CCC conscience sections, and the useful addition of Romans 8's 'no condemnation' as a reassurance pole. hyde_haiku has the best magisterial pairing for the mercy pole (VS §62 plus §104 on God's mercy and human weakness without falsifying the moral standard), but it is the most diluted: the attrition-versus-contrition article addresses a different sacramental question, and Augustine Section 18 on divine immutable goodness and the origin of evil is a genuine subject-matter drift reached through 'good/evil' vocabulary rather than any engagement with conscience. Its two Augustine chunks also add little beyond one another, and it omits CCC §1790–1794.

In short: hyde_cohere_haiku wins on precision and doctrinal balance but pays in redundancy and source breadth; hyde_cohere_luna wins on breadth and non-redundancy with slightly softer precision; hyde_haiku offers a distinctive mercy-pole text but the least disciplined retrieval.

judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines find the single most important passage — CCC §2709-2719 on contemplative prayer — so they differ mainly in what fills the remaining slots and how well they surface the second half of the query (universality vs. reservation to religious).

hyde_cohere_luna is the strongest overall. hyde_cohere_haiku is close behind. It has the same Catechism pair, the same Mediator Dei two-pole structure, and a well-chosen Summa Q180 a.8 on whether contemplation is continuous. Its weaknesses are ranking: Evangelii Gaudium §281 on intercessory prayer — a different form of prayer — is promoted to rank 4, while Matthew 6 is buried at rank 12, and the tail carries general moral-exhortation Scripture (Philippians 4, Colossians 3) and an Augustine Confessions chunk about preaching rather than contemplation.

hyde_haiku has the broadest angle coverage but the loosest concept discipline. It admits several passages that share only the word 'prayer': Ut Unum Sint §27 on praying for Christian unity, Clement VII.12 and Cyprian on petition and the Our Father, Psalm 4 as lament. It also duplicates Summa Question 182 (a.1 and a.4) making largely the same superiority-of-contemplation argument, and it misses Mediator Dei §174 and Matthew 6 — the two passages most directly answering the 'every Christian' half of the question — while retaining Mediator Dei §37, which alone tilts toward the 'reserved to religious' reading.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query asks why one would withdraw from active service of neighbor into contemplative/monastic life — the classic active vs. contemplative life tension. Strong direct hits: Luke 10 Martha/Mary (the locus classicus), ST II-II Q.182 A.1 (active vs. contemplative excellence), ST II-II Q.188 A.8 (solitary vs. community religious life), Redemptoris Missio §69 and Evangelii Nuntiandi §69 (consecrated life and mission), CCC §2709–2719 (contemplative prayer), Augustine's 'Work of Monks' section 38, Matthew 19 and Luke 14 (renunciation/counsels). Several chunks are weaker but still thematically plausible: Deus Caritas Est §40 on saints exercising charity (Martin of Tours, monk-bishop — tangential but touches the charity/monastic link), Deus Caritas Est §36 on the temptation of activism (adjacent, about the interior life of the charity worker — arguably relevant to why prayer is needed). Two clear drift items: CCC §2685–2690 on the family as first school of prayer / servants of prayer — this is about education in prayer, a different topic that shares 'prayer'/'contemplative' vocabulary, and it does discuss consecrated persons devoted to prayer in some editions, but the shown text is about the domestic church, which is not the concept asked about. Sirach 39 on the scribe who meditates on the law is a vocabulary/theme adjacency (study/meditation) rather than a treatment of withdrawal from the world. Clement Stromata IV.5 on abstinence from vicious acts is about martyrdom/abstinence rather than contemplative withdrawal. So there is meaningful topical drift in roughly three of fifteen slots — adjacency rather than a full wrong-doctrine collision, but the CCC family-prayer chunk in particular is a different subject matter retrieved on shared vocabulary.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection: Summa — found Q.182 A.1 ('Whether the active life is more excellent than the contemplative?'), which is the single most canonical passage in the corpus for this question, plus Q.188 A.8; excellent. Catechism — got CCC §2709–2719 on contemplative prayer (reasonable) but missed the canonical CCC §§914–933 on the consecrated life, and instead pulled §2685–2690 on family prayer, a peripheral slot; CCC selection is mid-tier at best. Deus Caritas Est — §36 and §40 are relevant to the charity/interior-life relation but the more canonical passage for this question is §7 (Gregory the Great on ascending to God and descending to neighbor), which was not found. Magisterial mission documents (Redemptoris Missio §69, Evangelii Nuntiandi §69) are apt canonical statements on consecrated life's missionary fruitfulness. Augustine 'De Opere Monachorum' §38 is a fitting close of that treatise. Overall strong on Summa and Scripture, weaker on Catechism and Deus Caritas Est.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The doctrinal tension here is: contemplation is objectively higher (Aquinas, Mary chosen the better part) versus charity toward neighbor is the measure of perfection and the contemplative life is not an escape but bears apostolic fruit; also that the lay/active life in the world is genuinely holy. The set captures the pro-contemplative pole strongly (ST Q.182 A.1, Luke 10, CCC contemplative prayer) and captures the fruitfulness/apostolic-integration pole via Redemptoris Missio §69, Evangelii Nuntiandi §69, Deus Caritas Est §36 and §40 (charity as irreplaceable), and Augustine on monks working. However, the explicit counter-pole that a life of activity in the world is fully compatible with sanctity (e.g., Mater et Magistra §255 or Christ's own choice of associating with men in ST III Q.40 A.1) is absent, and the ordering 'contemplata aliis tradere' / mixed life superiority is only implicit. Good but not fully balanced.
