judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines correctly read the query as the classical active-versus-contemplative-life question and converge on a shared scriptural core (Martha/Mary, the rich young man). They differ mainly in which authoritative treatments they surface and in how much tail noise they carry.

hyde_haiku has the single strongest systematic hit — Summa II-II Q.182 A.1, the corpus's canonical article on whether the active life is more excellent — and good mission-document coverage (Redemptoris Missio, Evangelii Nuntiandi). But its Catechism selection misses the consecrated-life sections entirely, substituting CCC §2685–2690 on family prayer, and it carries additional drift in Sirach 39 and Clement IV.5. It also lacks any passage explicitly affirming the holiness of the active life in the world, leaving the doctrinal picture the least balanced of the three.

hyde_cohere_haiku is the most precisely targeted: ST III Q.40 A.1 on why Christ associated with men rather than living in solitude, ST II-II Q.182 A.2 on comparative merit, Deus Caritas Est §7 on ascending to God and descending to neighbor, CCC §920–921, Laudato Si §126, and Mater et Magistra §255 together give both poles and every applicable angle. Its weakness is at the tail: two chunks from the identical Augustine De Trinitate chapter restating the same point, plus a synoptic Matthew/Mark duplication.

hyde_cohere_luna has the best magisterial/catechetical grounding — both CCC §920–921 and §931–933 from the consecrated-life treatment — and a very balanced doctrinal picture, but it never retrieves Q.182 A.1 or A.2, the most direct systematic comparison, settling for A.4 and Q.188 A.8. Its tail carries a Clement pair with overlapping substance and an Augustine De Trinitate chunk on love of neighbor that is a different doctrinal locus.

All three are pulled below 0.5 on relevance by tail chunks that share vocabulary (prayer, love of God and neighbor, detachment) while treating other subjects. On best-passage selection and doctrinal completeness the two cohere variants clearly outperform hyde_haiku; on redundancy hyde_haiku is cleanest because it avoids both the duplicated Augustine chapter and the synoptic duplication.

query: The Bible and Christian societies tolerated slavery. How can the Church claim moral authority after that?
rationale: development, dignity, and historical complicity; corpus-risk query

top.reference: Constitutions of the Holy Apostles — Book II. Of Bishops, Presbyters, and Deacons, Elucidation

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The core of the query is twofold: (a) biblical/historical toleration of slavery, and (b) whether the Church retains moral authority given doctrinal development. Chunk [1] Fratelli Tutti §86 addresses precisely the question of why the Church took so long to condemn slavery — a bullseye. [2]-[3] Magnifica Humanitas §§176–177 explicitly address past complicity in slavery and the anachronism problem — directly on point. [4] 1 Tim 6:1–2 and [7],[9] Deut 15 / Exod 21 are the actual biblical slavery texts the objection rests on — directly the evidentiary basis. [8] Irenaeus on the laws of bondage as pedagogical/temporary is squarely the classic development-of-revelation answer. [15] Divini Redemptoris §36 answers the accusation that the Church failed to live her principles — direct. [5]-[6] CCC 1929–1938 on human dignity and equality are the doctrinal ground for condemning slavery — relevant though more general social-justice framing. [11] and [14] Aquinas on slavery as punishment for sin and as matrimonial impediment are genuinely about slavery, though [14] is about marriage impediments (adjacent — it does supply the 'against nature in first intention' reasoning that is actually pertinent). [13] Augustine City of God XIX.15 is the canonical patristic treatment of servitude and sin — on point. [10] Leviticus 25 jubilee/redemption is on point scripturally. [12] Constitutions of the Holy Apostles elucidation on the Church gradually obliterating slavery is directly responsive to the historical-record angle. [16] Irenaeus IV.13 on the natural precepts not abrogated is thematically about law and development, weaker but not a wrong doctrine. No chunk represents a different doctrine masquerading via shared vocabulary; there is no vocabulary collision. A couple of chunks (CCC social justice, Irenaeus IV.13, Aquinas marriage impediment) are adjacent rather than central.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection: Fratelli Tutti — §86 is exactly the passage where Francis laments the delay in condemning slavery; canonical. Magnifica Humanitas — §§176–177 appear to be the document's direct treatment of slavery, complicity, and anachronistic judgment; canonical. Scripture — Exod 21, Deut 15, Lev 25, 1 Tim 6 are the four principal slavery loci; excellent selection (Philemon and Gal 3:28 / Col 3:11 would round it out, but the core texts are present). Summa — Q52 on the impediment of slavery and the Q189 reply on slavery as punishment for sin are the two places Aquinas actually theorizes servitude; reasonable, arguably the strongest available since the Summa has no dedicated 'is slavery licit' question. Augustine — City of God XIX.15 is the single canonical Augustinian passage on servitude; perfect. Irenaeus — IV.16 on the temporary pedagogical character of the laws of bondage is the right chapter; IV.13 is weaker/mid-tier. CCC — 1934–1938 (equality among men) and 1929–1933 (respect for the person) are strong; CCC §2414 (which explicitly names slavery as a sin against human dignity) and §1935/2298 would be the true canonical anti-slavery text and was missed. Divini Redemptoris §36 is the correct section defending the Church's historical record. Overall a strong-to-excellent selection with one notable CCC miss.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation (the biblical texts being objected to), historical precedent (the actual record of Christian societies and Church action), systematic/philosophical (why moral norms develop; nature vs. positive law), magisterial/conciliar (authoritative teaching on dignity and on the Church's authority), pastoral (how a believer holds this). Scriptural: Exod, Deut, Lev, 1 Tim — well covered. Systematic/philosophical: Aquinas ×2, Augustine XIX.15, Irenaeus on pedagogy of the law — richly covered. Magisterial: CCC ×2, Divini Redemptoris, Fratelli Tutti, Magnifica Humanitas — covered. Historical precedent: Constitutions of the Holy Apostles elucidation on the Church's gradual abolition of slavery, plus Divini Redemptoris's historical defense — covered. Pastoral: Fratelli Tutti and Magnifica Humanitas §177 (vigilance, call to responsibility) supply this. Five distinct angles genuinely represented.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The tension here is sharp: (a) the honest admission of complicity, delay, and blindness, versus (b) the defense of the Church's civilizing role and the legitimacy of doctrinal development. Both poles are strongly present: Fratelli Tutti §86 and Magnifica Humanitas §177 supply the penitential/self-critical pole; Divini Redemptoris §36 and the Constitutions elucidation on the Church gradually obliterating slavery supply the apologetic/historical-defense pole; Magnifica Humanitas §176 supplies the hermeneutical nuance (no anachronistic judgment, yet no minimizing). The scriptural pole is represented both by texts regulating slavery (Exod, 1 Tim) and by texts limiting/mitigating it (Deut 15 manumission, Lev 25 jubilee), which shows the internal trajectory. Augustine and Aquinas supply the older accommodationist framework, so the user sees what actually had to develop. What is thin is the explicit basis of magisterial authority itself (only lightly touched) and an explicit modern condemnation naming slavery intrinsically evil (CCC §2414 / Veritatis Splendor / Gaudium et Spes §27), which would close the loop. Still, both poles are genuinely present.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: Magnifica Humanitas §176 and §177 — sequential but doing different work (§176 hermeneutics of anachronism; §177 memory as call to present vigilance), so only mild overlap. CCC 1929–1933 and 1934–1938 — adjacent sections; the first on dignity of the person, the second on equality among men; related but substantively distinct arguments. Summa Q189 a.6 and Suppl. Q52 a.1 — different questions and different arguments (slavery as penalty for sin vs. slavery as against nature's second intention). Irenaeus IV.16 and IV.13 — both concern the Mosaic law's precepts and their abrogation/permanence; this is the closest to genuine same-source overlap, with IV.13 adding little beyond IV.16. Three Pentateuchal slavery laws (Exod/Deut/Lev) are different books, hence different sources, and each contributes a distinct provision. Overall low redundancy with one weak overlapping pair.

scores.summary: The strongest set: it pairs the exact self-critical magisterial passages (Fratelli Tutti §86, Magnifica Humanitas §§176–177) with the biblical texts the objection rests on, the patristic/scholastic accommodationist framework, the historical defense (Divini Redemptoris, Constitutions elucidation), and the CCC's dignity/equality basis. All five angles covered, both doctrinal poles present, minimal redundancy; only CCC §2414's explicit condemnation of slavery is conspicuously missing.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Strong core: Magnifica Humanitas §§176–177 directly address complicity in slavery and anachronistic judgment; the Constitutions elucidation directly addresses the Church's gradual abolition; Deut 15, Exod 21, Lev 25, 1 Tim 6 are the biblical slavery texts at issue; Irenaeus IV.16 on the laws of bondage is the development answer; Divini Redemptoris §36 answers the 'Church failed to live her principles' charge; Summa Suppl. Q52 on the condition of slavery is on-topic. However, [6] Summa II-II Q10 a.10 'Whether unbelievers may have authority or dominion over the faithful?' is a different doctrine entirely — it concerns the licitness of non-Christian rule over Christians and religious-liberty/dominion questions, retrieved because it shares the vocabulary 'authority,' 'dominion,' 'subjection,' and 'slave.' That is a textbook vocabulary collision on the word 'authority' in the query. Additionally [11] Irenaeus IV.13 here is the almsgiving/love-of-enemies passage, which has no bearing on slavery at all, and [14] CCC 2032–2040 is about the Magisterium's competence in moral matters generally — arguably relevant to 'moral authority' but it is the institutional-teaching-office section, not a treatment of the slavery problem. Also [13] Libertas §12 is on liberty and law broadly. The presence of a genuine wrong-doctrine chunk (II-II Q10 a.10) must pull this below the midpoint.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Magnifica Humanitas — §176 and §177 are the canonical passages; excellent. Scripture — Deut 15, Exod 21, Lev 25, 1 Tim 6: the right loci. Constitutions of the Holy Apostles — the elucidation on gradually obliterating slavery is the apt passage. Irenaeus — IV.16 is the correct chapter, but the second Irenaeus chunk (IV.13 on giving to those who take your coat) is a peripheral mention with no slavery content, a clear miss when Irenaeus has better material. Summa — Suppl. Q52 a.1 on slavery as an impediment is a defensible pick, but II-II Q10 a.10 on unbelievers' dominion is a peripheral/wrong pick, and the far better Aquinas passages (Q189 on slavery as penalty for sin, or the natural-law treatments) were missed. CCC — 2032–2040 on the Magisterium's moral competence is mid-tier at best for this query; the canonical CCC passages here are 1934–1938 (equality) and especially 2414 (slavery as a sin against dignity), neither of which was found. Divini Redemptoris §36 is the right section. Libertas §12 is thematically adjacent rather than core. Fratelli Tutti §86 — the single most on-point papal passage in the corpus — is entirely absent. Overall: good scriptural and Magnifica selection, but weak Summa, weak CCC, and a missed Fratelli Tutti.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural, historical precedent, systematic/philosophical, magisterial, pastoral. Scriptural: Deut, Exod, Lev, 1 Tim — well covered. Systematic/philosophical: Summa Suppl. Q52, Irenaeus IV.16 on the pedagogy of the law — covered, though thinner (no Augustine). Magisterial: Magnifica Humanitas, Divini Redemptoris, Libertas, CCC 2032–2040 — covered, and CCC 2032–2040 does supply the 'basis of the Church's moral teaching authority' angle the query implicitly raises. Historical precedent: Constitutions elucidation on the Church's gradual abolition, plus Divini Redemptoris's historical defense — covered. Pastoral: thinner — Magnifica Humanitas §177's call to vigilance is the main pastoral note; no Fratelli Tutti. Three or more genuinely distinct angles are present, with pastoral being the weak spot.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: Both poles are present but unevenly. The self-critical/penitential pole is represented by Magnifica Humanitas §§176–177 (complicity, blindness, need to ask pardon), and the defensive/authority pole is strongly represented by Divini Redemptoris §36, the Constitutions elucidation, Libertas §12, and CCC 2032–2040 on the Church's right to announce moral principles. Scripturally, both the regulating texts (Exod, 1 Tim) and the mitigating/manumission texts (Deut 15, Lev 25) appear, showing the internal trajectory. However, the balance tilts toward the apologetic/authority pole: the strongest admission of fault available in the corpus (Fratelli Tutti §86, 'we have no excuses,' 'it took so long') is absent, and the positive dignity basis (CCC 1934–1938 equality of all men, or an explicit condemnation of slavery) is also absent, so the reader gets the Church's defense and the Church's regret but not the developed doctrinal ground on which slavery is now condemned. The tension is represented, but one side is noticeably thinner.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: Magnifica Humanitas §176/§177 — sequential but making distinct points (anachronism hermeneutic vs. memory as call to vigilance), only mild overlap. Summa Suppl. Q52 and II-II Q10 a.10 — entirely different arguments, no redundancy. Irenaeus IV.16 and IV.13 — different chapters and here quite different content (laws of bondage vs. almsgiving/enemies), so not restating each other, though IV.13 is wasted for other reasons. Scripture chunks are from four different books, each with distinct provisions. No pair of same-source chunks restates the same substantive argument; result slots are wasted on irrelevance rather than on duplication, which is a relevance problem, not a redundancy one.

scores.summary: Solid scriptural and historical coverage with the key Magnifica Humanitas passages and Divini Redemptoris, and it uniquely surfaces CCC 2032–2040 on the Magisterium's moral competence. But it misses Fratelli Tutti §86, misses the CCC equality/dignity sections, and includes a clear vocabulary collision in Summa II-II Q10 a.10 on unbelievers' dominion over the faithful plus an irrelevant Irenaeus almsgiving passage — two wasted slots and a relevance failure.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The top of the ranking is excellent and well-ordered: Fratelli Tutti §86 (why so long to condemn slavery), Magnifica Humanitas §§176–177 (complicity, anachronism, vigilance), and Divini Redemptoris §36 (rebutting the charge that the Church betrayed her principles) are all bullseyes on the query's actual argumentative structure. CCC 1934–1938 (equality of all men) and 1939–1942 (solidarity) supply the dignity basis, with solidarity being somewhat more adjacent. Irenaeus IV.16, Augustine XIX.15, Exod 21, Deut 15, Lev 25, 1 Tim 6 are all genuinely about servitude. Clement's Instructor III.12 ('God is the same to free and bond') is a real patristic slavery-adjacent text. The weak spots: two chunks from Summa Suppl. Q39 a.3 on whether slavery impedes receiving Orders — this is a sacramental-discipline question about ordination, retrieved on the word 'slavery,' and it does not engage the moral licitness of slavery or the Church's authority at all; combined with Irenaeus IV.13 on natural precepts of the law, that is three of sixteen slots on material adjacent-to-off. I judge Q39 a.3 as peripheral-on-topic (it is literally about the state of slavery) rather than a wholly different doctrine, but it is the weakest kind of keyword match and one of the two chunks is a bare objection with no doctrinal content.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Fratelli Tutti — §86, the canonical passage; found. Magnifica Humanitas — §§176–177, the canonical treatment; found. Divini Redemptoris — §36, the right section defending the Church's record; found. CCC — 1934–1938 on equality among men is a strong choice and the closest thing to the dignity basis; 1939–1942 on solidarity is mid-tier; CCC §2414's explicit condemnation of slavery still missed. Augustine — City of God XIX.15, the canonical passage on servitude and sin; found. Irenaeus — IV.16 correct; IV.13 mid/peripheral. Scripture — Exod, Deut, Lev, 1 Tim: the right loci, though ranked very low (0.37–0.42), suggesting the pipeline undervalued the very texts the objection is built on. Summa — this is the clear failure: it selected Suppl. Q39 a.3 (slavery as impediment to Orders) twice, a narrow sacramental-discipline article, while missing Suppl. Q52 on the impediment of slavery to matrimony and II-II Q189's treatment of slavery as penalty for sin, both of which carry the actual Thomistic theory of servitude. Clement III.12 is a reasonable patristic find. Strong magisterial selection, weak Summa selection.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural, historical precedent, systematic/philosophical, magisterial, pastoral. Scriptural: Exod 21, Deut 15, Lev 25, 1 Tim 6 — covered. Magisterial: Fratelli Tutti, Magnifica Humanitas ×2, Divini Redemptoris, CCC ×2 — richly covered. Systematic/philosophical: Augustine XIX.15 on liberty and servitude introduced by sin, plus Aquinas (even if the articles chosen are narrow) and Irenaeus on the Mosaic law — covered. Pastoral: Fratelli Tutti §86, CCC on solidarity, Clement's Instructor on treating slaves with rebuke rather than punishment — covered. Historical precedent: thinner than the Luna set — Divini Redemptoris §36 gestures at the Church's historical record, but the Constitutions elucidation documenting the Church's gradual abolition of slavery is absent. Still, three-plus distinct angles are clearly and substantively represented.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: Both poles are represented and in fact this set balances them well at the top of the ranking: the penitential admission (Fratelli Tutti §86 'we have no excuses'; Magnifica Humanitas §177 on past complicity and blindness) sits directly alongside the apologetic defense (Divini Redemptoris §36 on the falseness of the accusation) and the hermeneutical nuance (Magnifica Humanitas §176 on not judging anachronistically while not minimizing). The positive doctrinal ground for the condemnation is supplied by CCC 1934–1938 on the equal dignity of all men and CCC 1939–1942 on solidarity. Scripturally, both the slavery-regulating texts and the manumission/jubilee texts appear, showing the trajectory within revelation. Missing: an explicit modern magisterial condemnation naming slavery as intrinsically evil (CCC §2414, Gaudium et Spes §27), and any account of the basis of the Church's teaching authority itself, which the query directly asks about. Both poles present with a modest gap.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: There is a clear redundancy failure: two chunks are drawn from the same Summa article, Supplement Q39 a.3 on whether the state of slavery impedes receiving Orders — one the Reply to Objection 3 about Paulinus, the other Objection 1 itself. These are fragments of a single article making the same point about corporal subjection and Orders, consuming two of sixteen slots for essentially one narrow argument. Beyond that: Magnifica Humanitas §176/§177 are sequential but do distinct work; CCC 1934–1938 and 1939–1942 are adjacent sections making related but distinct arguments (equality vs. solidarity); Irenaeus IV.16 and IV.13 are different chapters with different content. So one unambiguous same-source duplicated pair, with the remainder distinct.

scores.summary: Excellent magisterial core — Fratelli Tutti §86, Magnifica Humanitas §§176–177, and Divini Redemptoris §36 ranked at the top, capturing both the admission and the defense — plus Augustine, Clement, and the CCC dignity sections. Undermined by its Summa handling: two fragments of the same narrow article on slavery as an impediment to Orders, which is both peripheral and redundant, and it ranks the key biblical slavery texts implausibly low.

judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines converge on a strong shared spine: Magnifica Humanitas §§176–177 (the Church's own reckoning with complicity in slavery and the warning against anachronistic judgment), Divini Redemptoris §36 (rebutting the charge of failing to live her principles), Irenaeus IV.16 (the Mosaic laws of bondage as pedagogical and temporary), and the core biblical slavery loci (Exod 21, Deut 15, 1 Tim 6). That shared core already answers the question's two halves — the scriptural evidence and the logic of doctrinal development — so the pipelines are differentiated almost entirely by their unique additions.

hyde_cohere_luna is the strongest overall. It is the only set that simultaneously secures Fratelli Tutti §86 (the single most directly responsive papal passage: 'I sometimes wonder why... it took so long'), the CCC's dignity and equality sections as the positive doctrinal ground, Augustine's City of God XIX.15 as the canonical patristic treatment of servitude, the Constitutions of the Holy Apostles elucidation documenting the Church's gradual abolition of slavery (the historical-precedent angle no other pipeline covers as well), and two substantively different Aquinas articles. It hits all five applicable angles, holds both poles of the tension in balance, and contains no wrong-doctrine retrieval — only mild adjacency in Irenaeus IV.13 and the marriage-impediment article.

hyde_cohere_haiku has an arguably better-ordered top four than Luna — it ranks Fratelli Tutti, Magnifica Humanitas ×2, and Divini Redemptoris as its first four hits, which is precisely the argumentative skeleton of a good answer — and it adds Clement of Alexandria and the CCC solidarity section. But it degrades badly at the tail: it spends two slots on fragments of a single Summa article about whether slavery impedes ordination (a narrow sacramental-discipline question, redundant with itself and peripheral to the moral question), it misses the better Aquinas material on servitude that Luna found, it drops the Constitutions historical passage, and it ranks the biblical slavery texts at 0.37–0.42, implausibly low for the very passages the objection is built on.

hyde_haiku is the weakest. It misses Fratelli Tutti §86 entirely, misses the CCC equality/dignity sections, and commits the one unambiguous vocabulary collision in the evaluation: Summa II-II Q10 a.10, 'Whether unbelievers may have authority or dominion over the faithful?' — a different doctrine about non-Christian rule over Christians, retrieved on the shared tokens 'authority,' 'dominion,' and 'slave' from the query's phrase 'moral authority.' It compounds this with an Irenaeus IV.13 chunk about almsgiving and loving enemies that has no bearing on slavery at all. Its distinctive contribution is CCC 2032–2040 on the Magisterium's competence in moral matters, which no other pipeline retrieved and which does speak to the query's 'claim moral authority' clause — a genuine insight — but it leaves the set tilted toward institutional self-defense with the strongest available admission of fault absent.

On redundancy the ranking inverts relative to relevance: hyde_haiku wastes slots on irrelevance rather than duplication and so scores highest, while hyde_cohere_haiku is the only pipeline with a true same-source duplicated argument. Ranking overall: hyde_cohere_luna > hyde_cohere_haiku > hyde_haiku.

query: Did the Church change its teaching about religious freedom, or did Vatican II contradict earlier popes?
rationale: development versus contradiction; councils-dependent corpus-risk query

top.reference: Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part (Second Part of the Second Part) (Qq. 1–189), Question 1 - Of Faith (Ten Articles), Article 7 - Whether the articles of faith have increased in course of time?

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query has two components: (a) the substance of religious-freedom teaching, and (b) whether doctrinal development amounts to contradiction. Chunks 1, 2, 5 (CCC §160, Redemptor Hominis §17 on Dignitatis Humanae, CCC §2101–2109 on the natural right and its due limits) hit the substance directly. Pacem in Terris §14 is the immediate pre-conciliar magisterial groundwork for DH — squarely on point. Ut Unum Sint §18 and Veritatis Splendor §1 (quoting John XXIII's 'deposit of faith is one thing, the manner of its expression another') address the development-vs-contradiction hermeneutic directly, which is the second half of the query. The two Summa II-II q.10 a.8 chunks on compelling unbelievers/heretics are the genuine pre-modern coercion position the query implicitly contrasts — relevant, not a collision. Irenaeus on human liberty as free agency is patristic background, somewhat looser but engages freedom of the act of faith. The two Origen Against Celsus chunks (natural law vs. written law of cities, Mosaic vs. Christian legislation) are the weakest: they concern law and civil obedience generally, drifting toward an adjacent topic rather than religious liberty as a right, and they occupy two of eleven slots. No outright wrong-doctrine collision, but two peripheral drifting chunks plus a loose patristic one.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection: CCC — §2101–2109 is essentially the canonical Catechism treatment of religious liberty (drawing on DH) and §160 on freedom of faith; both are core, good selection. Redemptor Hominis §17 is exactly where JPII treats DH and religious freedom — canonical. Pacem in Terris §14 is the key rights passage. Ut Unum Sint §18 is a genuinely apt passage on reformulating doctrine without altering the deposit. Veritatis Splendor §1 chunk, however, is a footnote/citation fragment rather than substantive text — a mid-to-low tier retrieval from that document. Summa: II-II q.10 a.8 is precisely the canonical Aquinas article on compelling unbelievers, though only the Replies to Objections were pulled rather than the corpus/'I answer that', so it is the right article but a secondary slice of it. Origen chunks are peripheral within Contra Celsum for this question. Notably absent: Dignitatis Humanae itself as a primary text, and Immortale Dei / Quanta Cura / Syllabus — the earlier papal texts that the query alleges were contradicted; the corpus clearly contains at least the Syllabus and Immortale Dei (they appear in sibling pipelines), so a clearly relevant collection was missed entirely. Overall a solid but incomplete best-passage record.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: conciliar/magisterial definition, systematic/philosophical reasoning, historical precedent (earlier papal condemnations, patristic practice), pastoral application; scriptural foundation is marginally applicable. Coverage: magisterial/conciliar is strong (CCC, Redemptor Hominis on DH, Pacem in Terris, Ut Unum Sint, Veritatis Splendor); systematic reasoning present via Aquinas on coercion; historical/patristic precedent via Irenaeus and Origen. That is three or more genuinely distinct angles. The weak spot is that the historical precedent angle covers the patristic era but not the 19th-century magisterial pole (Gregory XVI, Pius IX, Leo XIII) that the question is really about — so the 'earlier popes' historical angle is thinner than ideal, but it is not absent as an angle type since Aquinas and the Fathers supply pre-conciliar voices.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: This query is defined by doctrinal tension: the 19th-century condemnations of 'liberty of worship' (Mirari Vos, Quanta Cura, Syllabus, Immortale Dei) versus Dignitatis Humanae's affirmation of a civil right to religious freedom, mediated by the development-of-doctrine hermeneutic. This set represents the affirming pole richly (CCC, DH via Redemptor Hominis, Pacem in Terris) and supplies the hermeneutical key (Ut Unum Sint §18, the John XXIII deposit/expression distinction in Veritatis Splendor). It also gives a genuine coercive counter-pole via Aquinas ('heretics should be compelled to keep the faith'), and CCC §2101–2109 supplies the important nuance about 'due limits' and the rejection of a positivist conception of religious liberty. What is missing is the actual earlier papal magisterium being asked about — no Syllabus, no Immortale Dei, no Quanta Cura — so the user cannot see what was in fact condemned and thus cannot evaluate the alleged contradiction. Aquinas partially substitutes but is not the papal pole. Dominant side well covered; the balancing magisterial pole is thin.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: two Summa chunks from the identical article (II-II q.10 a.8) — Reply to Obj. 1 (slaying/compelling heretics, Augustine's change of mind) and Reply to Obj. 3 (accepting faith is voluntary, keeping it obligatory). These are adjacent but make distinguishable points, though both restate the same core thesis that heretics may be coerced; substantial overlap. Two Origen Contra Celsum chunks (Bk V ch. 37 and Bk VII ch. 26) both argue essentially the same thing — divine/natural law versus the written law of cities and the legitimacy of departing from civil law — clear same-source restatement. Two same-source overlapping pairs out of eleven slots is more than a single mild overlap.

scores.summary: Strong magisterial coverage of the affirming pole plus a genuine development-of-doctrine hermeneutic (Ut Unum Sint, Veritatis Splendor) and an Aquinas coercion counter-pole, but the actual 19th-century papal texts the question alleges were contradicted are absent, and two Origen chunks plus a duplicated Summa article dilute precision and add redundancy.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Directly on-target: Redemptor Hominis §17 (DH and religious freedom), CCC §160 (freedom of the act of faith), CCC §2101–2109 (natural right, due limits), and Syllabus of Errors §79 — the latter is the single most pointed retrieval in any pipeline for the 'did earlier popes teach the opposite?' half of the query. Magnifica Humanitas §§33–34 address Vatican II as a turning point and John XXIII's rights language: relevant to development, though they speak about the Council's social-teaching orientation in general rather than religious liberty specifically. The Summa II-II q.1 a.7 chunk on whether articles of faith increase over time is a genuinely apt systematic treatment of doctrinal development, though only the Reply to Obj. 2 fragment. The Summa II-II q.1 a.10 chunk on whether the Sovereign Pontiff may draw up a symbol of faith and the conciliar prohibition on new creeds is a vocabulary-adjacent drift: it concerns the authority to formulate creeds, not religious freedom or doctrinal reversal, and reads as a collision on 'council'/'faith' language. Irenaeus on human liberty is loose patristic background. So one clear off-target chunk and two general-development chunks.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: CCC: §2101–2109 and §160 are the canonical Catechism loci — good. Redemptor Hominis §17 is the canonical JPII passage on DH. Syllabus of Errors §79 is precisely the proposition on civil liberty of worship at issue — an excellent, canonical selection of the opposing pole. Magnifica Humanitas §§33–34 are relevant but mid-tier framing sections rather than a direct treatment of religious liberty. Summa: q.1 a.7 is the right article for development of doctrine but only a Reply fragment rather than the substantive 'I answer that'; q.1 a.10 is a poor selection from Aquinas given that II-II q.10 a.8 (compelling unbelievers) is demonstrably in the corpus and far more apposite. Dignitatis Humanae itself is again absent as a primary source, and no Immortale Dei/Quanta Cura to accompany the Syllabus. Mixed: two canonical hits and one excellent historical hit, offset by weak Summa selection.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: magisterial/conciliar definition, systematic reasoning, historical precedent, pastoral application. Magisterial: strong (CCC, Redemptor Hominis, Magnifica Humanitas). Historical precedent: strongest of the three pipelines via Syllabus §79 plus Irenaeus. Systematic: present via Aquinas on development of the articles of faith (and, weakly, on creedal authority). Pastoral: Magnifica Humanitas on the Church close to humanity gestures at it. Three or more distinct applicable angles are genuinely covered, including the historical pole other pipelines partly miss.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: This set uniquely holds both poles in explicit tension: Syllabus of Errors §79 states the 19th-century condemnation of civil liberty of worship, while CCC §2101–2109, CCC §160 and Redemptor Hominis §17 present the conciliar affirmation, and CCC §2109 supplies the 'due limits' nuance that prevents a libertarian misreading. Magnifica Humanitas and Aquinas on whether articles of faith increase over time give the developmental hermeneutic that reconciles them. What is missing relative to an ideal set is a magisterial statement of the development/continuity hermeneutic itself (e.g., Ut Unum Sint §18 or the deposit/expression distinction) and Dignitatis Humanae's own claim that it is developing rather than reversing prior teaching. Still, a user reading this set would see both sides of the alleged contradiction and a route to reconciliation.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: Magnifica Humanitas §§33 and 34 are consecutive sections both narrating the modern development of social teaching/rights language — related and adjacent, with §33 on John XXIII and §34 on Gaudium et Spes, so they make distinguishable historical points but with noticeable thematic overlap. The two Summa chunks are from different articles (q.1 a.7 and q.1 a.10) making clearly different arguments — not redundant. CCC chunks are from different, distinct sections. Overall only one mildly overlapping same-source pair.

scores.summary: The only pipeline to surface the Syllabus of Errors alongside the conciliar affirmation, giving the best doctrinal balance for a 'did teaching change?' question; weakened by an off-target Summa chunk on papal authority to draft creeds and by mid-tier Magnifica Humanitas framing sections in place of Dignitatis Humanae itself.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Very high on-topic density. CCC §2101–2109 and §160 address religious liberty and the freedom of faith directly. Immortale Dei §34 is exactly on point for the 'earlier popes' pole, explicitly recounting Gregory XVI's Mirari Vos and the condemnations of liberty-of-worship doctrines. Pacem in Terris §14 is the pre-conciliar rights foundation; Redemptor Hominis §17 treats DH explicitly; Ut Unum Sint §18 supplies the reform-of-formulation-without-altering-the-deposit hermeneutic. Summa II-II q.1 a.7 ('I answer that' on implicit/explicit articles of faith) is the substantive systematic account of development; II-II q.10 a.8 gives the coercion counter-pole. Irenaeus is loose patristic background on liberty. The two Origen chunks on natural law versus the written law of cities remain the weakest — adjacent civil-law material rather than religious freedom as such. No wrong-doctrine collision, but two peripheral slots.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: CCC: §2101–2109 (canonical) and §160 — both core. Immortale Dei §34 is a genuinely canonical passage for Leo XIII's restatement of the prior condemnations. Pacem in Terris §14 is the key rights text. Ut Unum Sint §18 is the apt passage on legitimate reformulation. Summa: this pipeline pulled the substantive 'I answer that' from q.1 a.7 on whether the articles of faith increase — the best available Aquinas passage on development — plus the right article (q.10 a.8) on compelling unbelievers, though only a Reply fragment. Redemptor Hominis §17 is canonical for DH. The persistent gap across all pipelines is Dignitatis Humanae itself, and here the Syllabus is absent (though Immortale Dei covers similar ground). Origen chunks remain peripheral selections from Contra Celsum. Overall the strongest per-collection selection of the three.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: magisterial/conciliar, systematic/philosophical, historical precedent, pastoral. Magisterial is dense and spans eras (Immortale Dei, Pacem in Terris, Redemptor Hominis, Ut Unum Sint, CCC). Systematic reasoning is well served by two Aquinas passages, one on development of articles of faith and one on coercion. Historical precedent covers both the 19th-century papal pole (Immortale Dei) and the patristic era (Irenaeus, Origen). Three or more distinct applicable angles are robustly covered; only a distinctly pastoral-application voice and scriptural foundation are thin, and the latter is marginal for this query.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: Both poles are present and the bridge between them is explicit. The restrictive pole: Immortale Dei §34 recounting the papal condemnations of liberty of worship, plus Aquinas that heretics may be compelled to keep the faith. The affirming pole: CCC §2101–2109, CCC §160, Pacem in Terris §14, Redemptor Hominis §17 on DH. The reconciling hermeneutic: Ut Unum Sint §18 on reforming the manner of formulating doctrine without altering the deposit, and Summa q.1 a.7 on the implicit-to-explicit growth of articles of faith. CCC §2109 also supplies the 'due limits' nuance restraining a purely liberal reading. The main residual gap is Dignitatis Humanae's own self-understanding as continuous development; otherwise this is a near-complete picture of the tension.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: the two Summa chunks are from different questions and articles (q.1 a.7 on development; q.10 a.8 on coercion) making entirely different arguments — not redundant. The two CCC chunks are distinct sections on distinct points. The two Origen Contra Celsum chunks (Bk V ch. 37 and Bk VII ch. 26), however, both argue substantially the same thesis about natural/divine law versus the written law of cities — a clear same-source restatement occupying two slots. Everything else is single-source and distinct.

scores.summary: The most complete set: dense magisterial coverage across eras, Immortale Dei supplying the pre-conciliar pole, Ut Unum Sint and the substantive Summa passage on development of the articles of faith supplying the reconciling hermeneutic; marred only by a redundant pair of tangential Origen chunks.

judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines share a solid magisterial core (CCC §160, CCC §2101–2109, Redemptor Hominis §17 on Dignitatis Humanae, Irenaeus on human liberty), so differentiation turns on whether each surfaced (a) the pre-conciliar restrictive pole the question alleges was contradicted, and (b) a hermeneutic of development to reconcile the two.

hyde_cohere_luna performs best overall: it alone pairs Immortale Dei §34 (Leo XIII rehearsing Gregory XVI's condemnations) with Ut Unum Sint §18 and the substantive 'I answer that' from Summa II-II q.1 a.7 on the growth of the articles of faith — precisely the affirmation, counter-pole, and reconciling principle the query requires. Its only real defect is a redundant pair of tangential Origen Contra Celsum chunks.

hyde_haiku is the only pipeline to retrieve the Syllabus of Errors §79, arguably the single most probative text for this question, and it avoids the Origen drift entirely, giving it the cleanest redundancy profile. But it spends two slots on mid-tier Magnifica Humanitas framing sections and one on Summa II-II q.1 a.10 (papal authority to draft a symbol of faith), which is an off-target drift on shared 'faith/council' vocabulary and displaces the far more apposite q.10 a.8 that both sibling pipelines found.

hyde_cohere_haiku is the weakest: it retrieves the development hermeneutic (Ut Unum Sint, plus the John XXIII deposit/expression distinction embedded in a Veritatis Splendor footnote fragment) but omits every 19th-century papal text, leaving the 'earlier popes' side represented only by Aquinas on compelling heretics. It also carries two redundancy problems — two Replies from the same Summa article and the same duplicative Origen pair — making it the least efficient use of eleven slots.

A gap common to all three: Dignitatis Humanae itself never appears as a primary text, despite being the document explicitly named in the query.

query: Why did Christians once condemn charging interest as usury when modern economies depend on lending?
rationale: object and circumstance across changed economic structures

top.reference: Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part (Second Part of the Second Part) (Qq. 1–189), Question 78 - (E) By Sins Committed in Loans (Q. 78), Article 1 - Whether it is a sin to take usury for money lent?

Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part (Second Part of the Second Part) (Qq. 1–189), Question 78 - (E) By Sins Committed in Loans (Q. 78), Article 1 - Whether it is a sin to take usury for money lent?

Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part (Second Part of the Second Part) (Qq. 1–189), Question 78 - (E) By Sins Committed in Loans (Q. 78), Article 1 - Whether it is a sin to take usury for money lent?

Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part (Second Part of the Second Part) (Qq. 1–189), Question 78 - (E) By Sins Committed in Loans (Q. 78), Article 1 - Whether it is a sin to take usury for money lent?

Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part (Second Part of the Second Part) (Qq. 1–189), Question 78 - (E) By Sins Committed in Loans (Q. 78), Article 1 - Whether it is a sin to take usury for money lent?
Cyprian. — The Treatises of Cyprian., Book III · Testimony XLVIII

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Top results directly engage usury: Aquinas ST II-II Q.78 A.1 (twice, the corpus's canonical systematic treatment), Vix Pervenit §§7 and 10 (the definitive magisterial condemnation and the explicit rebuttal of the 'modern economy makes usury obsolete' claim — precisely the query's tension), Cyprian's testimony 'that we must not take usury,' Nehemiah 5 (exacting usury from brethren), Deuteronomy 23 and 15 (the Mosaic lending/interest prohibitions and debt release), and Clement's Stromata on lending. Caritas in Veritate §§37, 65 and CCC §§2426–2436 / 2437–2442 are the modern-economy side — genuinely relevant to why lending is now legitimate and how finance must be morally ordered, though they never name usury; they are adjacent rather than collisions since the query explicitly asks about modern economies. The one weak chunk is Exodus 22:16–31, retrieved apparently for the dowry/sorceress/legal-miscellany material at the chunk's start; the passage does contain the 'if you lend money to my people, you shall not charge interest' verse later in Ex 22, so it is topically germane but the retrieved excerpt shows unrelated cultic and sexual-morality law, making it a near-miss on precision rather than a wrong doctrine. No chunk addresses a different doctrine entirely.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Summa: found ST II-II Q.78 A.1 corpus (the respondeo plus a reply) — the exact canonical locus on usury; ideal. Vix Pervenit: §§7 and 10 — the encyclical's core condemnation plus the section directly answering 'usury is only nominal today'; ideal. Scripture: Deut 23 and Deut 15 and Neh 5 are the standard Old Testament loci, though the Deuteronomy 23 chunk buries the interest verse in a long legal miscellany and Leviticus 25 (the fullest OT treatment of lending to the poor without increase) was missed; Exodus 22 chunk is off-window. Patristics: Cyprian's Testimony XLVIII is literally titled 'That we must not take usury' — canonical; Clement Stromata II.18 does treat lending law. Caritas in Veritate §§37 and 65 are strong finance/economy sections. CCC: §§2426–2442 on economic activity and justice among nations is the closest the Catechism gets, reasonable though the Catechism has no dedicated usury treatment. Overall a strong canonical hit rate with a couple of mid-tier scriptural windows.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation, systematic/philosophical reasoning, conciliar/magisterial definition, historical precedent (patristic/medieval development), and pastoral/contemporary application. Scriptural: Deut 15, Deut 23, Neh 5, Ex 22. Systematic: Aquinas on selling what does not exist and consumptibles. Magisterial: Vix Pervenit (Benedict XIV) plus CCC. Historical/patristic: Cyprian, Clement. Contemporary pastoral application: Caritas in Veritate on finance and the real economy. Five distinct angles genuinely represented.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The doctrine has real tension: the absolute condemnation of usury versus the modern legitimacy of interest (money as productive capital, extrinsic titles, Vix Pervenit §3's own concession that other titles of gain may licitly accompany a loan). The condemnation pole is very strong (Aquinas, Vix Pervenit §§7, 10, Cyprian, Torah). The resolving pole is only partially present: Caritas in Veritate §§37 and 65 legitimize finance as an instrument and CCC §2426ff affirms lawful economic activity and profit, which does gesture at the development; and Aquinas's Reply to Obj. 5 touches compensation questions. But the crucial nuance — Vix Pervenit's own distinction admitting licit titles, the 1917/1983 canonical permission of legal interest, or the productive-capital rationale — is not explicitly retrieved, so the 'why interest is now licit' side remains inferential rather than documented.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Two Summa chunks from the same article, but they are distinct: the respondeo's core argument about selling nonexistent use versus Reply to Obj. 5 on repayment according to equality of justice — complementary, not restating. Two Vix Pervenit sections differ (general scriptural condemnation vs. rebuttal of the contemporary objection). Two Caritas in Veritate sections differ (§37 justice in all economic phases vs. §65 reform of finance), and the two CCC chunks cover economic activity vs. international debt — adjacent but each adds content. Scriptural chunks are from different books except the two Deuteronomy passages, which cover different material (interest prohibition vs. sabbatical debt release). Minor thematic overlap only.

scores.summary: The strongest set: canonical Aquinas and Vix Pervenit passages including the section that directly confronts the 'usury is only nominal today' objection, full patristic and scriptural grounding, and contemporary social-doctrine material on finance. Weakened slightly by an off-window Exodus 22 chunk and by not surfacing the explicit doctrinal basis on which interest later became licit.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Aquinas ST II-II Q.78 A.1 appears twice, including Reply to Obj. 2 which is directly germane (Jews forbidden usury from brethren, extended to all men in the Gospel state) — squarely on the query's historical-development axis. Vix Pervenit §§7 and 10 again hit the condemnation and the explicit modern-economy objection. judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines share a strong spine: Aquinas ST II-II Q.78 A.1, Vix Pervenit §§7 and 10 (including the section that directly rebuts the claim that usury is merely nominal in a commercial economy), Cyprian's dedicated usury testimony, Clement, and the Torah/Nehemiah prohibitions. They therefore all achieve full multi-angle coverage — scriptural, systematic, magisterial, patristic-historical, and contemporary-pastoral — and all share the same doctrinal gap: none surfaces the passages that would explain how interest became licit (extrinsic titles, Vix Pervenit's own concessions, canonical permission of moderate interest), so each documents the condemnation far better than the development the question presupposes.

They diverge on tail precision. hyde_cohere_luna keeps the strongest ranking (Aquinas and Vix Pervenit at the top) and pairs the condemnation with genuinely economic modern sources (Caritas in Veritate §§37, 65; CCC §§2426–2442), spoiled only by an off-window Exodus 22 chunk. hyde_cohere_haiku matches it in coverage and adds Leviticus 25 and the valuable Aquinas Reply to Obj. 2, but wastes a slot on the CCC 'In Brief' summary that duplicates its own §2426–2436 chunk, lowering its redundancy score. hyde_haiku retrieves the single most useful Aquinas reply for this query (human law tolerating usury for the imperfect) but drifts hardest at the tail, filling three to four slots with almsgiving and gratuitousness material (Cyprian Treatise VIII, CCC §2443–2449, Caritas in Veritate §34) that concerns charity rather than interest, and it also ranks the scriptural miscellany above the magisterial sources. Net: luna is the most precise, cohere_haiku the most complete but slightly redundant, and haiku the least precise despite one standout systematic find.

query: If Church leaders have sometimes been corrupt or disastrously wrong in practice, why trust the Church to teach reliably?
rationale: teaching reliability versus personal holiness and governance

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: The query asks why the Church's teaching authority can be trusted despite corrupt or mistaken leaders. This pipeline's top chunks engage the question with unusual precision: Mystici Corporis §66 directly addresses human weakness in the Church without impugning her divine constitution; CCC §888–892 and CCC §85–87 explain the teaching office and Magisterium; Summa II-II q.1 a.9 gives the exact principle 'the universal Church cannot err, since she is governed by the Holy Ghost'; Summa II-II q.2 a.6 grounds faith in Divine truth rather than human knowledge (the person/office distinction); Matthew 23:1–36 is the classic 'do what they say, not what they do' scriptural warrant; Irenaeus on presbyters with the charism of truth plus the accompanying chunk on unworthy leaders both fit. Mediator Dei §19, Commissum Divinitus §4, and Qui Pluribus §10 all bear on the Church's divine mandate to teach and the need for a living authority against private judgment. 1 Corinthians 4:1–5 (stewards judged by the Lord, not human courts) and 1 Timothy 3:15 ('pillar and ground of the truth') are apt. Weaker: 2 Timothy 2:14–26 is generic exhortation about handling the word and avoiding disputes — thematically adjacent rather than on the trust-despite-corruption question; Ignatius Eph. XVI on those who corrupt the faith by wicked doctrine is about heretics corrupting families, a related-but-different concern; Cyprian Ep. LXXIII on heresies and schisms arising is about schismatic baptism/authority disputes rather than magisterial reliability. These are drift, not a wrong-doctrine collision — no chunk is about an entirely different doctrine that merely shares vocabulary. Overall high relevance with two or three peripheral items.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Per collection: Catechism — both CCC §85–87 (the Magisterium section, arguably the canonical answer passage on why the teaching office is trustworthy) and CCC §888–892 (bishops' teaching office and infallibility conditions) are core treatments; excellent. Summa — q.1 a.9's 'the universal Church cannot err' is precisely the canonical Thomistic statement, and q.2 a.6 supplies the 'rule of faith is Divine truth, not human learning' point; strong. Encyclicals — Mystici Corporis §66 is the single best magisterial passage in the corpus on scandal by even 'the most exalted members' not derogating from the Church's holiness; Qui Pluribus §10 on God establishing a living authority is on point; Commissum Divinitus §4 on the divinely instituted magisterium is good, though Mediator Dei §19 is a mid-tier liturgical-context mention of the Church's teaching function. Scripture — Matthew 23 is the canonical passage; 1 Tim 3:15 and 1 Cor 4 are apt; 2 Tim 2 is mid-tier. Patristics — Irenaeus IV.26 is the canonical patristic locus (charism of truth in succession, and the warning about presbyters who serve their own pleasure); Cyprian LXXIII and Ignatius XVI are peripheral. Averaging, most relevant collections are represented by their strongest passages.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural foundation, systematic/philosophical reasoning, conciliar/magisterial definition, historical precedent (patristic experience of unworthy bishops), and pastoral application (how a scandalized believer should respond). Scriptural: Matthew 23, 1 Cor 4, 1 Tim 3, 2 Tim 2. Systematic: two Summa articles on the Church's inerrancy and the rule of faith. Magisterial: CCC §85–87, CCC §888–892, Mystici Corporis, Mediator Dei, Commissum Divinitus, Qui Pluribus. Historical/patristic: Irenaeus (two chunks), Cyprian, Ignatius. Pastoral is the thinnest, though Mystici Corporis §66 carries a pastoral consolation function. Four distinct angles are genuinely and substantively covered.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The doctrine here has a real tension: the Church's indefectibility and the assistance of the Spirit in teaching, versus the sinfulness and fallibility of individual pastors and the limits of what is guaranteed (infallibility is not impeccability, and not every prudential act or disciplinary decision is protected). This set captures the affirmative pole abundantly (Magisterium, cannot err, obey presbyters, living authority). The balancing pole is present but partly implicit: Mystici Corporis §66 names weakness even in exalted members; Matthew 23 and Irenaeus's warning about unworthy presbyters and Cyprian's account of lapsed bishops acknowledge real corruption; 1 Cor 4 places stewards under God's judgment. What is thin is an explicit articulation of the limits of infallibility — the distinction between the guaranteed object of infallible teaching and non-infallible prudential governance, and the CCC §827/§823–829 'holy yet always in need of purification' semper purificanda theme, which the sibling pipeline surfaced. So the nuance is represented but not with the sharpest available texts.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: two Irenaeus Against Heresies IV.26 chunks — but these make different arguments (one on the charism of truth in apostolic succession, the other on Samuel's blameless stewardship as a measure for presbyters who abuse office), so this is complementary rather than duplicative. Two CCC chunks are different sections making distinct points (Magisterium's interpretive authority vs. bishops' teaching office). Two Summa chunks are different questions with different theses. The three nineteenth-century/papal texts (Commissum Divinitus §4, Qui Pluribus §10, Mediator Dei §19) are different documents, so convergence rather than redundancy, though Commissum Divinitus and Qui Pluribus advance a very similar 'God established a living teaching authority' point. Minimal wasted slots.

scores.summary: The strongest overall set: it pairs the canonical magisterial and Thomistic statements of the Church's inerrancy with the specific texts that concede human corruption (Mystici Corporis §66, Matthew 23, Irenaeus, Cyprian), spanning four angles with little redundancy. Slight relevance drift at the tail (2 Tim 2, Ignatius, Cyprian LXXIII) and a thin explicit treatment of the limits of infallibility.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: This set leans heavily toward the 'corrupt leaders' half of the query and under-serves the 'why trust the teaching' half. Strong hits: Matthew 23:1–36, CCC §823–829 (the Church is holy yet includes sinners and is semper purificanda), Mit Brennender Sorge §19 (divine mission obscured by human failings — an excellent fit), CCC §888–892, Veritatis Splendor §27, Cyprian Ep. LXVII (bishops guilty of grave crimes cannot validly rule), Irenaeus IV.26 (both chunks), Summa II-II q.2 a.6. But there is substantial drift: Luke 11:37–54, Mark 12:38–40, and Luke 12:1–3 are three additional Pharisee-hypocrisy pericopes that merely echo Matthew 23 and speak to hypocritical religious leaders in general, not to the epistemic question of trusting the Church's magisterium. Summa II-II q.11 a.2 on whether heresy is properly about matters of faith is a different doctrinal question (the definition of heresy and culpability) that shares 'faith/error' vocabulary — this reads as a vocabulary collision, drawn in by 'the Church being wrong' language but addressing the delimitation of heresy rather than magisterial reliability. Ecclesiam Suam §47 on reform not meaning change is adjacent (renewal) rather than on-point. Cyprian Treatise I §17 on not being disturbed by the faithlessness of many is loosely pastoral. Because at least one chunk addresses a genuinely different doctrinal question under shared vocabulary, and several others are keyword-driven Pharisee passages, relevance is materially compromised.

best_passage_selection.reasoning: Catechism: CCC §823–829 (the Church is holy) is a genuinely excellent and arguably canonical passage for the 'sinners in a holy Church' pole, and CCC §888–892 covers the teaching office — but the most direct answer passage, CCC §85–87 on the Magisterium's authority, is missing, and it clearly exists in the corpus since two other pipelines found it. Summa: q.2 a.6 is decent, but the pipeline missed q.1 a.9's 'the universal Church cannot err' — the single most canonical Thomistic passage for this query — and instead retrieved the heresy question, a poor selection. Encyclicals: Mit Brennender Sorge §19 is a strong, aptly chosen passage; Veritatis Splendor §27 is solid on the Apostles' entrusted task; Ecclesiam Suam §47 is mid-tier. Gospels: Matthew 23 is canonical, but the three parallel Pharisee passages are peripheral duplicative selections rather than better texts. Patristics: Irenaeus IV.26 is the canonical locus and both chunks were found; Cyprian LXVII is a reasonable historical case, Treatise I §17 is peripheral. Overall: good passages in some collections, clearly better available passages missed in the two most important ones.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural, systematic, magisterial, historical precedent, pastoral. Scriptural is heavily covered (four Gospel passages). Magisterial: CCC §823–829, CCC §888–892, Mit Brennender Sorge, Veritatis Splendor, Ecclesiam Suam — well covered. Historical/patristic: Cyprian (two) and Irenaeus (two) — covered, including concrete historical cases of criminal bishops. Systematic: only Summa q.2 a.6 plus the off-target heresy article, so philosophical treatment of the Church's inerrancy is thin. Pastoral: Mit Brennender Sorge and Cyprian's Treatise I §17 ('let not the faithlessness of many disturb us') supply this. Three or more distinct angles are genuinely present, with scriptural over-weighted and systematic underweighted.

doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: This set is notably strong on the nuance pole — the Church contains sinners, is always in need of purification (CCC §823–829), her mission is obscured by human failings (Mit Brennender Sorge), bishops have committed grave crimes (Cyprian LXVII), leaders say and do not do (four Gospel passages). But the affirmative pole — why the teaching itself is nonetheless reliable — is comparatively thin: it rests mainly on CCC §888–892 and Veritatis Splendor §27, with the decisive 'the universal Church cannot err because governed by the Spirit of truth' and the Magisterium's authority (CCC §85–87) both absent. A user reading only this set would grasp that the Church admits corruption but would get a weaker account of the ground of trust, which is precisely what the query asks. So it is the inverse imbalance of the other pipelines: both poles present, but the affirmative side under-supported.

redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source redundancy is the visible weakness here. Matthew 23:1–36, Luke 11:37–54, Mark 12:38–40, and Luke 12:1–3 are all Gospel/Synoptic denunciations of Pharisaic hypocrisy making essentially the same substantive point — hypocritical religious leaders — occupying four of fifteen slots; if one treats the Gospels as a single Bible source these are near-restatements of one another. The two Cyprian chunks (Ep. LXVII on criminal bishops, Treatise I §17 on not being disturbed by faithlessness) make different points, and the two Irenaeus IV.26 chunks are complementary, and the two CCC chunks are distinct. But the Synoptic pile-up wastes multiple slots.

scores.summary: Best coverage of the 'corrupt leaders' pole — CCC §823–829 and Mit Brennender Sorge §19 are excellent finds — but it misses the canonical trust-grounding passages (CCC §85–87, Summa q.1 a.9), pulls in an off-target Summa article on heresy, and burns four slots on interchangeable Pharisee pericopes.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Nearly every chunk engages the specific question of why the Church's teaching can be trusted notwithstanding bad leaders. Mystici Corporis §66 addresses human weakness in even the most exalted members; CCC §85–87 gives the Magisterium's authority; Summa q.1 a.9 states 'the universal Church cannot err'; Summa q.2 a.6 distinguishes human learning from Divine truth as the rule of faith; CCC §888–892 on the teaching office; Lumen Fidei §49 on apostolic succession guaranteeing continuity and certain access to the wellspring of faith — a precise fit; Veritatis Splendor §27 on the task entrusted to the Apostles' successors; Matthew 23 the canonical scriptural warrant; Irenaeus IV.26 both chunks; Qui Pluribus §10 on God's establishment of a living authority against private judgment; 1 Tim 3:15 'pillar and ground of the truth'; 1 Cor 4:1–5 on stewards judged by the Lord; Cyprian LXVII on criminal bishops. Weaker tail: 2 Timothy 3:10–17 is about persecution, evil times, and the usefulness of Scripture — adjacent exhortation rather than the trust question; Cyprian LXXIII on heresies and schisms is about schismatic authority disputes. best_passage_selection.reasoning: Catechism: both §85–87 (Magisterium) and §888–892 (teaching office) — the two core treatments; excellent. Summa: q.1 a.9's 'the universal Church cannot err, since she is governed by the Holy Ghost' is the canonical Thomistic answer, plus q.2 a.6; excellent. Encyclicals/magisterial: Mystici Corporis §66 is the single best passage on scandal without derogation from the Church, Lumen Fidei §49 and Veritatis Splendor §27 are core treatments of transmission and the entrusted teaching task, Qui Pluribus §10 on the living authority; very strong. Scripture: Matthew 23 canonical, 1 Tim 3:15 apt, 1 Cor 4 apt, 2 Tim 3 mid-tier. Patristics: Irenaeus IV.26 both chunks (the canonical locus), Cyprian LXVII a good concrete historical case, Cyprian LXXIII peripheral. Missing only CCC §823–829 on the Church as holy yet in need of purification. Across collections this is close to the best available selection.

multi_angle_coverage.reasoning: Applicable angles: scriptural, systematic, magisterial/conciliar, historical precedent, pastoral. Scriptural: Matthew 23, 1 Tim 3, 2 Tim 3, 1 Cor 4. Systematic: two Summa articles going directly to the Church's inerrancy and the rule of faith. Magisterial: CCC (two sections), Mystici Corporis, Lumen Fidei, Veritatis Splendor, Qui Pluribus — including Veritatis Splendor's citation of Vatican II. doctrinal_completeness.reasoning: The affirmative pole — divine assistance, indefectibility, apostolic succession, the Magisterium's Christ-given authority — is very fully represented. The balancing pole is present: Mystici Corporis §66 explicitly concedes evil even in exalted members, Matthew 23 concedes leaders who say and do not do, Irenaeus's second chunk sets Samuel's blameless stewardship against presbyters who abuse office, Cyprian LXVII shows bishops guilty of apostasy and grave crimes, and 1 Cor 4 subjects stewards to divine judgment. Still missing is an explicit statement of the limits of the guarantee — that infallibility is not impeccability and does not cover prudential governance or disciplinary decisions — and CCC §823–829's 'holy yet always in need of purification,' which the corpus demonstrably contains. redundancy_rate.reasoning: Same-source pairs: two Irenaeus IV.26 chunks making complementary rather than identical arguments (charism of truth in succession vs. the standard of blameless stewardship for presbyters); two Cyprian epistles making distinct points (criminal bishops cannot rule vs. heresies fostered by misplaced advocacy); two CCC sections that are distinct treatments; two Summa articles from different questions with different theses; 1 Cor 4, 1 Tim 3, and 2 Tim 3 are three different Pauline passages with different emphases (stewardship/judgment, the Church as pillar of truth, endurance and the utility of Scripture). scores.summary: Very close to the strongest set: it assembles the canonical trust-grounding passages (CCC §85–87, Summa q.1 a.9, Lumen Fidei §49) alongside the texts conceding real corruption (Mystici Corporis §66, Matthew 23, Cyprian LXVII, Irenaeus), across four angles with almost no redundancy. Only 2 Tim 3 and Cyprian LXXIII drift, and CCC §823–829's purification theme is missed.

judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines share a strong core (Matthew 23, CCC §888–892, Summa II-II q.2 a.6, and both Irenaeus IV.26 chunks), so the differentiation lies entirely in the unique retrievals — and the two halves of this query pull in opposite directions.

hyde_cohere_luna and hyde_cohere_haiku converge on the same winning strategy: they pair the canonical grounds of trust (CCC §85–87 on the Magisterium, Summa q.1 a.9's 'the universal Church cannot err, since she is governed by the Holy Ghost') with the single best magisterial concession of leadership corruption (Mystici Corporis §66 on evil 'even at times in the most exalted members'). That combination is exactly the shape of the question. luna adds Lumen Fidei §49 and Veritatis Splendor §27 on apostolic succession as the guarantee of continuity, and 2 Tim 3; cohere_haiku adds three papal texts on the divinely instituted living magisterium (Commissum Divinitus, Qui Pluribus, Mediator Dei) plus Ignatius and 2 Tim 2. luna's tail is marginally cleaner and it also captures Cyprian LXVII's concrete case of criminal bishops, which cohere_haiku lacks; cohere_haiku's Commissum Divinitus/Qui Pluribus pairing is somewhat repetitive in argument even though from distinct documents. The two are near-equivalent, with luna slightly ahead on relevance and passage selection.

hyde_haiku pursues the opposite emphasis and pays for it. It uniquely surfaces two of the best 'sinful Church' passages in the corpus — CCC §823–829 (holy yet always in need of purification) and Mit Brennender Sorge §19 (the divine mission obscured by 'human, too human' failings) — which neither sibling found, and it is the most honest about the corruption pole. But it misses both canonical trust-grounding passages that its siblings located, substitutes an off-target Summa article on the definition of heresy, and spends four slots on interchangeable Synoptic Pharisee denunciations (Matthew 23, Luke 11, Mark 12, Luke 12) that restate one point. The result answers 'yes, leaders have been corrupt' far better than 'so why trust the teaching' — the actual question — and its redundancy and relevance scores reflect that.

Ideal set would be luna's core plus hyde_haiku's CCC §823–829 and Mit Brennender Sorge §19, and none of the three surfaced an explicit statement that infallibility is not impeccability and does not extend to prudential governance — the sharpest available resolution of the tension.

retrieval_relevance.reasoning: Most chunks engage the specific grace/merit relationship directly: CCC §2006–2011 is the Catechism's merit section; Augustine ch. 107 ('eternal life, though the reward of good works, is itself the gift of God') is precisely the paradox; ST I-II q.114 a.3 (condign merit) and a.5 (cannot merit first grace) are the systematic core; Eph 2:1–10, CCC §1996–2005 on grace, Augustine ch. 30 and Moral Treatises §17 on merit not preceding grace, Phil 2:12–18 ('work out your salvation... for it is God who works in you'), Mt 10:41–42 on reward, James 2:14–26 on faith and works, and Mediator Dei §36 on divine action and human cooperation all address the question. The tail is weaker: Lumen Fidei §19 (0.38) is about sonship/faith and only tangentially about merit; Spe Salvi §44 concerns the Last Judgment and hope in divine justice — related to reward eschatology but not to merit-vs-grace; Mediator Dei §31 is about sacramental efficacy and dispositions, a different doctrine (ex opere operato/sacramental fruitfulness) that shares the word 'grace.' That last one is closest to a vocabulary collision, though it does touch cooperation with grace rather than a wholly foreign doctrine. judge.comparative_analysis:
All three pipelines converge on the same doctrinal spine — CCC §2006–2011 (merit) plus CCC §1996–2005 (grace), Summa I-II q.114, Augustine's anti-Pelagian treatises, Ephesians 2, and Mediator Dei §36 — so all three achieve full doctrinal completeness (both the gratuity pole and the reality-of-merit pole, with the Catechism's 'crowning his own gifts' synthesis) and full multi-angle coverage (scriptural, systematic, magisterial/catechetical, patristic, pastoral).

They separate on the finer dimensions. hyde_cohere_haiku has the best best-passage selection because it alone retrieves Summa q.114 Article 1, 'Whether a man may merit anything from God?', which is almost a verbatim restatement of the query, alongside both Catechism sections; its weakest picks (Origen on free will, Mediator Dei §78) are adjacent rather than wrong. hyde_cohere_luna has an equally strong head (CCC merit section at rank 1, ST a.3 and a.5) but a soft tail of three low-scoring chunks, notably Mediator Dei §31 on sacramental efficacy and Spe Salvi §44 on the Last Judgment, which share grace/justice vocabulary without treating merit.

hyde_haiku has the broadest scriptural coverage (adding Hebrews 6:10 and 2 Cor 6:1, both genuinely apt) but suffers most on relevance and redundancy: the 'Quod Hoc Ineunte' jubilee preamble is a clear off-topic retrieval driven by incidental vocabulary, Lumen Fidei §19 is ranked implausibly high at 0.92, and four Augustine chunks largely restate the same 'even faith/free will/love is God's gift' argument, wasting result slots that the other two pipelines spent on distinct sources.

Net: hyde_cohere_haiku is the strongest overall, hyde_cohere_luna close behind with a weaker tail, and hyde_haiku the weakest on precision and non-redundancy despite comparable doctrinal breadth.
